speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Minister of Employment and Immigration) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-62
speechtext:
That, in relation to Bill C-62, an Act respecting employment equity, one sitting day shall be allotted to the consideration of the second reading stage of the said Bill; and
That 15 minutes before the expiry of the time provided for the consideration of government business on the above-mentioned sitting day, any proceedings then before the House shall be interrupted, if necessary, for the purpose of this Order and, in turn, every question necessary to dispose of the said stage of the said Bill shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
She said: Mr. Speaker, almost a year ago on November 20, 1984, I tabled in this House the report of Judge Rosalie Abella on equality in employment. Very shortly after that, in fact within days, almost within hours, opposition Members were demanding and pleading that the Government give its response to the Abella royal commission report. That was a year ago. In March of 1985 I had the privilege and honour of presenting the Government's response in principle. At that time I promised that legislation would be introduced shortly. Still, the Opposition got up and demanded immediate action with regard to legislation. The Opposition said: "Bring it in within the next few days, within the next few weeks".
Sir, the legislation was presented on June 28 of this year. Along with it we presented a working paper which was designed to stimulate wide-ranging consultation and debate throughout the summer months. That, indeed, took place. Mr. Speaker, second reading debate on Bill C-62 has been under way since October 3. In other words, what I am explaining to the House is that this particular piece of legislation has been received, delivered, analysed, scrutinized and debated for the better part of a year. Thoughout all of that time there has been intense consultation with business, the target groups, unions, individuals and organizations right across the country. More consultation, more discussion and more debate will follow at committee stage. Therefore, it is time to move this Bill forward, Mr. Speaker.
Hon. Members opposite have indeed made points and we have attempted to answer them. Then they made the same points over again. This circuitous discussion on equity, of course, is not new. This sort of thing has been going on for years and years until the Government has the courage to introduce this specific, practical, employment equity legislation.
I have listened to those who say that the legislation does not go far enough and I have listened to those who say that it goes much too far. It would be nice if one could please all of the people all of the time, but, Mr. Speaker, we live in a real world. The new legislation is a realistic effort to solve the employment problems that are faced by women, native people, disabled persons and visible minorities.
First, this Bill seeks to attain what is attainable. It establishes a mandatory reporting requirement on larger firms under federal jurisdiction which employ 100 or more workers. That, in effect, will have impact on over one million Canadians. Second, in addition to the mandatory reporting requirement, the Bill makes effective use of existing enforcement agencies and resources. In fact, the Bill brings these agencies into operation for the first time in order to ensure compliance based on results. We do not need to create new enforcement bureaucracies when the Canadian Human Rights Commission already has the power to ensure that investigation and enforcement is carried out.
I may say that this approach is well in line with one of the options recommended by Judge Abella in her report. Under Model 4 of the enforcement mechanisms in her report Judge Abella suggests that the Canadian Human Rights Commission would be responsible for issuing employment equity guidelines, for collecting, reviewing and assessing data, for investigating and adjudicating disputes, and for contract compliance. Mr. Speaker, we are doing things very much in line with the proposals of Judge Abella. The Canada Employment and Immigration Commission is preparing equity guidelines and will offer consultative services to the firms involved. Similarly, we will ensure that data is collected and we will make it available to the Canadian Human Rights Commission as well as to individuals, groups and organizations across the country. The Canadian Human Rights Commission, in following up on this data, will handle the investigation and adjudication of disputes about employment equity, such as is recommended in the Judge Abella's Report. Section 32.3 of the Canadian Human Rights Act, legislation which is already in force, empowers the Canadian Human rights Commission to initiate complaints where reasonable grounds exist. The mandatory data collected as a result of Bill C-62 will provide the grounds for investigations.

The data that employers will be required to provide under the legislation will be specific and clear enough to ensure effective enforcement. No one will be able to cover up employment discrimination once this Bill goes into effect.
The Government will provide the Canadian Human Rights Commission with the resources necessary to conduct effective investigations. We believe that by using an existing agency rather than creating a new one, we save precious tax dollars and cut down on administrative overhead and overlapping responsibilities. More to the point, we use an agency which has already proven its worth and which has shown to the Canadian people that it can be effective in safeguarding equality and helping to eliminate discrimination in this country.
Contract compliance procedures are also in place. I might point out that these procedures do not require legislation but only the will of the Government to write into the contracts it has with business the requirements that will be necessary. It makes eminent sense to require enterprises that wish to do business with the federal Government to live up to employment equity standards. That has been done. We are doing that by requiring that all contracts for $200,000 or more be backed up by employment equity plans. Canada Employment and Immigration Commission officials will monitor these contracts and advise the contracting Minister about companies who do not live up to their commitments. The result of that may be that the companies will be barred from doing future business with the Government.
I believe that these enforcement and compliance measures will ensure that employers live up to the spirit and the intent of the new law. I would like more time to speak on this particular matter but I realize that my time is indeed limited. I believe that we have reason to be optimistic.
While the opposition Members have spent much time criticizing the legislation, they seem to agree that employment equity is an important and vital objective. Some members in the Opposition claim that it does not go far enough. However, I ask them what they did in previous years. This Government is the first to have the courage to take action in this field and implement new, strong legislation for employment equity. It is time to move this Bill forward. It is time to get on to the next step in this process. The people of this country want and need employment equity. We want to give it to them.

Mr. Speaker, I want to preface my remarks this morning by indicating to the House that at the international conference held in New York some seven or eight days ago, the international reporting group indicated that the existing legislation, not Bill C-62, is among the most innovative and creative legislation in the western world dealing with women's problems.
As the Minister indicated earlier, there is no doubt that there were complaints about the record of the previous Liberal administration. I can assure the House that when I finish my
remarks the Minister will understand that I believe certain portions of this Bill are not strong enough. However, when one examines the previous Government's commitment to the enhancement of the quality of the workplace and the payments related to it, I suggest one will find that the previous Government's record will stand on its own. Furthermore, that record is recognized by the international community.
The Minister is quite correct in saying that there will be representatives of various groups in our society who believe very strongly that Bill C-62 does not address the problems that were dealt with in the Abella Commission's Report to the Government of Canada. These groups which indicate that the Government's response to the Abella Report is far too meagre to be discussed this morning represent a majority of women in this country. These groups include the Canadian Labour Congress, the Urban Alliance on Race Relations and the Canadian Congress for Learning Opportunities for Women. These groups represent a majority of women in this country.
These are the same groups which appeared before the Abella Commission. They represent women, disabled people and members of visible minorities in this country. They stated that there is a need for mandatory affirmative action programs to overcome the inequalities that women experience in the Canadian labour force. They said: "Those mandatory affirmative action programs must be backed up by strong and effective enforcement procedures if we are to see progress toward equality".
Therefore, one of their first criticisms of Bill C-62 is that the Government has not opted for mandatory affirmative action programs.
A second concern is the monitoring process. The Minister indicates that she believes that the Canadian Human Rights Commission has had an excellent track record and should not be concerned about its ability to ensure that the intent of the legislation will be enforced. However, the Bill only requires employers to report the data on their workforce by sex, race and disability. Not only do we maintain a reporting relationship, I believe the Bill indicates that the Government will do little with these reports until 1988. There will be a three year delay while the Government reviews the reporting relationships from these various data bases before any action is taken.
It has been clear in past years that when a Government simply indicates it wants to have a reporting relationship rather than providing strong and effective legislation, it does nothing to address the immediate inequalities that exist in the workforce. Furthermore, while public reporting is useful and should continue, it is important that the Government act on that information once it has been collected. When one considers that there will be a three year delay in accumulating the reporting information, and when one considers the past record of the Canadian Human Rights Commission, 1 suggest it will be the year 2000 before we see the first test case before the Supreme Court.
The point made by these groups to the Abella Commission was that the purpose of affirmative action programs is to move away from the complaints system, to which I just alluded.
November 18, 1985

which places the onus for change on the victims of discrimination. Instead, the onus should be placed where it properly belongs, that is, on the employment systems themselves. We are saying that the reporting stage is only the first step and the Bill should provide greater ability for the Government to respond to inequalities that exist in our workforce.
Before I go into the specifics of the Bill, let me refer to a statement made by the Canadian Labour Congress. It state that it has been possible to file complaints regarding failure to pay equal pay for work of equal value for almost 10 years now. But this complaint system has not been very effective in bringing pay equity to women. It is already law. As an example, federal sector employers should be required to provide equal pay for work of equal value in their establishments.

The Government's Bill today does not require this. The onus remains on women to make their employers obey the law. That is a serious flaw in the legislation, Mr. Speaker.
As I have indicated in moments past the complaint system itself has been far too slow and has not yet addressed the systemic discrimination that exists in the workforce toward women.
Let me indicate some other areas where we believe serious flaws exist in Bill C-62. First, Judge Abella herself recommended four alternative enforcement mechanisms to ensure that employment equity is implemented. The Government indicates that the Human Rights Commission, with no formal extension of its own mandate or of its funding, will both monitor and enforce the program. There again that is a very serious flaw. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the backlog in cases before the Canadian Human Rights Commission is sufficient now that there are serious doubts whether the CHRC can fulfil the kind of mandate that Bill C-62 will give it unless its funding mechanism and mandate are extended to deal with it effectively.
Second, the extension of employment equity to federally regulated business will exclude companies with fewer than 100 employees. In effect, what we are talking about is excluding roughly 82 per cent of companies that do business with the federal Government, which is the intent of Bill C-62. With only 18 per cent of companies required to enforce these regulations, I really do wonder about the commitment which the Conservative Government has to address the inequality that takes place now in the workforce with respect to women.
Let us now look at Government contracts for goods and services. I mentioned earlier that employment equity will only apply to those companies with more than 100 employees and to contracts over $200,000. In other words, it means that effectively you have eliminated the need for small business to adhere to the new regualations under Bill C-62.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has indicated on the floor of the House previously that the majority of jobs being created today, never mind the existing pattern, are created by small business.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words on the time allocation Bill brought before the House by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald).
I want to oppose the motion brought before the House for many of the same reasons which the Minister herself used to oppose these motions when in Opposition. I can recall the Minister making statement after statement as an opposition Member saying that this represented a guillotine and did not give the House proper time to consider a particular Bill. I can quote speech after speech of hers. She has a very short memory. If she were on this side of the House she would resent being pushed around by the Prime Minister's Office and by the Government House Leader.
We have had only a few days of debate on Bill C-62 since it was brought before the House. We had a debate on October 3, October 21, on October 23, on October 30 and on October 31. That is five days, but in reality we had only four days. On October 30 only one speech was made. The second speaker moved adjournment of the House and the bells rang for the rest of the day. We have had four days of debate on this legislation. Is four days of debate long enough on an issue as important as employment equity for the women of Canada, for native people, for visible minorities and for the handicapped? The answer to that is no, it is not long enough.
Our Party has had 14 Members speak on this Bill, the Liberal Party has had a comparative number, and Conservative Party Members have not been anywhere near as involved.
To me it is passing strange that a Conservative Government that spoke in opposition about openness, consultation and national reconciliation would spend only four days on an issue

as important as employment equity before bringing down the guillotine. It is not fair at all.
This is an important issue to women, to the visible minorities, to the native people and to the physically handicapped. We have to make sure that we have strong legislation to make sure these people have opportunities for employment equity. The program in the Minister's Bill is not adequate. She said we can accomplish these things through a voluntary method of affirmative action in Canada, but that is not the case.
Judge Abella in her report said that we need mandatory affirmative action. The Americans have been saying that for years. Let me read to the House a statement made by Judy Lichtman, Executive Director of the Women's Legal Defence Fund in Washington, D.C. At a conference the other day here in Canada she said that she was dubious about affirmative action programs that do not have fixed goals for employers. She said:
In our American experience, we got no compliance until there was an enforcement mechanism.
We do not have an enforcement mechanism in this Bill and that is what this debate is all about. Everything is voluntary. In the United States they do have such a mechanism. But until there was something mandatory in the U.S. there was no compliance. Miss Lichtman went on to say:
Under U.S. law, firms doing business with the federal Government cannot discriminate by gender and must meet deadlines and targets for hiring women.
In Canada, in this Bill, we do not have any targets, deadlines, objectives, goals or quotas in terms of affirmative action by companies from which the federal Government buys supplies and goods. Miss Lichtman went on to say:
A court can order companies with more than 15 employees to take affirmative action measures.
In this Bill the program applies only to companies that have over 100 employees that do business with the federal Government. In the United States, a much bigger country, the American can make companies with 15 employees or more comply. Why can we not do the same here with companies with 15 or more employees and make this rule mandatory? If that were the case, we would not be having this debate in the House of Commons. The Bill would have gone to committee after a couple of days for detailed study and analysis.
This is the fourth time we have had a time allocation motion in this House since September, that is four time allocation motions in the last two months. I am concerned about that as a parliamentarian. What was in the past an occasional practice is becoming a custom under the Conservative Government of Canada of bringing in time allocation time and time again. Before long this will become a custom and a convention. I do not think that is good for an open and free democratic parliamentary system.
Also, in the last while we have had rule changes. Now, compared with the past, we have 20-minute speeches with a 10-minute question period. After a certain amount of time expires, we are down to 10-minute speeches. There is less need
to have a closure motion or a time allocation motion than there was in the past. I recall what members of the Conservative Party have been saying in the House in the last 15 years after the Liberals brought in time allocation motions after several days of debate. They said that it was the guillotine and that the House had not had enough time to deliberate. In those days we had longer speeches. We would go on for several weeks, such as in the case of the Crow debate, before time allocation was brought in. The Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) would rise in the House as an opposition Member and talk about how horrible it was that democracy was being chocked or cut off.
One reason the Conservatives are losing popularity faster than any other Government in the history of Canada is that they have misled Canadians. They have not been honest with Canadians as to where they stand. They said one thing in Opposition; they do another thing in Government. We have another example of that today. While in opposition, they talked about full and fair debates, free-ranging debate and several days of debate. They would rise and be very angry at the Government for cutting off debate. However, once they are in Government, the table is turned; it is a different tale. I think that is why Canadians are becoming very dismayed by the Conservative Party which sits across the way. That is why we are seeing in the House what will become, in my opinion, a one-term Government.

That has been the legacy of the Conservative Party in the last 14 months since they won the Government of Canada. That is why the people of the country are losing trust and confidence in the Government sitting across the way.
I appeal to Hon. Members of the Conservative Party, even those on the back-benches, to rise and speak their minds. They should not be pushed around by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald). They should not be afraid of the Prime Minister of the country. He will not be there very long. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this debate, and thus bring the second reading stage to an end and refer the Bill to committee according to our normal procedure.
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak today, and not because I feel we are suppressing individual freedom of speech. On the contrary, Mr. Speaker, we will have ample opportunity within the legislative committees to make our points and to indicate to the Government the amendments we would like to see in this legislation. There is certainly no shame in doing so, and I do not think we are to be criticized for following this procedure.
Mr. Speaker, I may point out that we previously considered a similar Bill in the House. The Bill went to the legislative committee, where we considered again the same motions that had been presented before the House, and I just realized now that when the Bill comes back to the House, we will again be considering the same motions that were presented in committee after first being presented in the House.
Members of the public listening to us this morning and on other occasions often say, and I think we should listen: There is a lot of repetition and a lot of redundancy.
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate, because basically, our Bill is based on two concepts:
Time Allocation
trust and performance. We want, and our friends opposite have always wanted to have a system with public servants to run it. We will make a plan and develop it, and penalties will be provided.
Canadians must be told how to achieve legitimate objectives that are set by a government, whatever its political affiliation. Our friends opposite always thought: Not only are we going to give you a plan, we have an objective and we gave you a plan. That is how things were, Mr. Speaker, because we were not working according to a Government plan and that is how people were kept in a state of inferiority.
Mr. Speaker, this must be true because when our friends opposite talk about women in the House, they are always talking about them in connection with their place in society, with family allowances and pension plans. They are kept in a state of inferiority and they are not given the information they should be given, and that is the kind of role our friends opposite have made women play. We want to do better than that.
Mr. Speaker, we are going to set objectives, and we are going to start by cleaning our own backyard. We are going to set general objectives, and then we are going to compare performances from year to year. And that is what we are going to measure. We are not going to measure a plan set up by a public servant. We are going to measure performance.
Mr. Speaker, we must stop telling Canadians: This is what we want. We must tell them: Here is the recipe for achieving what we want to achieve.
Mr. Speaker, the other day 1 was listening to the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) when he said: There was one important measure in the Budget, and that was the rebate on ... that is to say, Canadians would not be paying taxes on profits, on capital gains over four or five years. But he said: Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, Canadians were not told how to spend the money they would save in the process, and these people are going to invest that money elsewhere.
That shows the difference between our two parties, Mr. Speaker. The party opposite would have said: We are granting a tax rebate on capital gains, but we are also going to tell you what you have to do with the money. This Government is saying: Here is a tax rebate, and we think Canadians are smart and clever enough to know what to do with the money they will save. That is the difference in our philosophies.
Mr. Speaker, it takes a plan based on performance, not a plan set up and run by public servants. That is the essential thing: a plan based on confidence in the public. Instead of being a public servant run plan, it will consist of a public plan and reports that will be tabled in Parliament. We are hearing reactions from the various associations, and that is how it should be. We are now hearing from these various associations across Canada. Some support the Government's action and others do not criticize it except to say it does not go far

enough. But even with this legislation which, according to the Opposition, does not go far enough, we are going much further than you ever did in the last fifteen years.
Mr. Speaker, these organizations will be able to have input in a Government plan and in an office or a commission, and they would not have had that right before, while today, the plan is public, it will be released to the public, and even the Canadian Human Rights Commission will be able to intervene legally as required in certain cases. Not only it will be able to do so, but it will also have to hear individuals or pressure groups which will want to be heard on the matter.
Mr. Speaker, this is the thrust of this Bill. We are ready to discuss it in legislative committee. We are ready to hear once again the views of the Opposition. However, we have to say that this is a constructive measure. The legislation now in effect is the first step. The usual criticism is that it does not apply to all businesses. Mr. Speaker, firstly, we begin by cleaning our own house. Secondly, we proceed by groups or targets and on the basis of performances. The eligible groups will be in a position to resort to self-scrutiny and self-control because discrimination is not a legal issue. First and foremost, it is a matter of attitude and openness. And Canadians, both men and women, have made some progress since then.
Mr. Speaker, 1 spent a week in a riding where 1 visited an Indian reserve. Its leaders are telling the Government that it is urgent to act as far as employment equity is concerned.
All this, Mr. Speaker, still is a matter of confidence and I mean confidence at the level of Canadian businesses and businessmen and not confidence in the plan put forward by the Government. Confidence in businesses on the basis of their performances from one year to another. This is the basic issue. This is the reason why I am pleased to support this Bill and to say: We will now go to the legislative committee to consider and further discuss the subject matter of Bill C-62.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like Canadians to understand the Government's initiative which rests on action-not a voluntary one-aimed at drawing a logical plan for each business. In that respect, the voluntary aspect will not allow the company to choose the direction of its plan, because the direction or the target have already been chosen. As far as means and performances are concerned, year after year, Canadians are mature enough to review them without necessarily relying on a Government plan providing all criteria.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased-and sad-to take the floor on this Bill dealing with an issue which I think should have been given a lot more attention.
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that for the first time women, disabled persons and native people are quite justified to feel that the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has let them down.
Mr. Speaker, not only is the Government promoting a Bill which reflects the approach of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Government-a hypocritical approach- but at best this is a half-baked measure like all the others. Hon. Members need only recall the deindexation of old age security pensions, the deindexation of family allowances and the 10 per cent tax on sick Canadians. And now we are considering this feeble attempt at a Bill, when for years on end women, disabled persons and native people have been fighting to gain full recognition in terms of employment equity. This Government can only come up with second-class measures.
Mr. Speaker, we Canadians now have laws for second-class women, laws for second-class disabled persons, and laws for second-class native people. Any women lucky enough to get a job with a company having more than 100 employees soon finds out that she rates minimal protection, what we might call token protection.
But if she happens to be one of fewer than 100 employees she does not have any protection at all. That, Mr. Speaker, tells us all about our Prime Minister. The Hon. Member who just resumed his seat, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Hudon), could only keep repeating that it is a matter of confidence, Mr. Speaker. Obviously he got up too early to read this morning's newspapers, otherwise he would know that the latest Gallup poll indicates that 52 per cent of Canadians no longer have confidence in this Government, 52 per cent of them disagree with Government policies after only one year since it came into office. Worse still, Mr. Speaker, most people do not even know what this Bill is all about, so you can imagine how they will react when they do find out what the Government has in store for them!
I have to say that the women who successfully ran under the Conservative Party banner are nobodies! Mr. Speaker, the Coalition des femmes du Quebec met with Quebec women Conservative MPs only to be told that they did not want to be associated with the case of women. That is not what they had promised, Mr. Speaker. Is there one Hon. Member who will try to have me believe that women will be protected if they get jobs with companies having more than 100 employees? Most women who work as waitresses in the restaurant industry will not be protected under this measure, Mr. Speaker. This is where they are being exploited, Mr. Speaker, but the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) would rather bury her head in the sand like an ostrich and heed the advice of the Minister of Finance instead of standing on her own two feet and advocating the kind of Bill she personally favours. If the Tories keep this up, Mr. Speaker, 75 and even 80 per cent of Canadians-not only 52 per cent-will turn against this Government.
Is it acceptable that, in 1985, human beings elected to represent their fellow citizens introduce a Bill for the purpose of granting a minimum protection based on the status or
November 18, 1985

corporation, Mr. Speaker? It reminds me of the Government's Bill concerning the spouse allowance for widows and widowers. Half measures all, Mr. Speaker. If you are single, you are not entitled to it; if you are separated, you are not entitled to it. They create classes of citizens. They have just the Prime Minister's image, just a clean-cut guy with a nice slogan, very nice on the surface but without substance, Mr. Speaker.
When I think of the promises that were made by this Government, 1 recall the debate which Canadian women had organized during the election campaign; how great our dear Prime Minister looked, with such an open-mindedness and so many firm promises. 1 can understand that Conservative Members are anxious to limit the length of the debate, for they are ashamed to see what the Government is proposing now compared to what it had promised; 1 can understand that Conservative women are ashamed and dare not rise to deal with this issue. I can understand that, because if I were they, 1 should be ashamed too to defend this Bill, in view of all the promises their Party had made to the Canadian people.
What will be the end result of this Bill, Mr. Speaker? From now on, companies willing to do so will submit a report to the Government, and a bunch of civil servants will compile the relevant data. On the proper forms, company so and so will state: I have over 100 employees. Last year, I had not a single woman on my staff. This year, I have one. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a certain irony in the efforts of the opposition Members to delay the passage of Bill C-62 dealing with employment equity. This irony, I am sure, is not lost on the Canadians most in need of the positive measures put forward in this Bill, that is, native people, disabled people, members of visible minority groups, and the women of Canada's workforce. Canadian women in particular must find this whole exercise of nit-picking especially ironic. The two decades which have passed since women surged in record numbers into the workforce is a period distinguished by a singular lack of practical action on employment equity from various Liberal Government incarnations. Instead, what Canadians got was a lot of studies, commissions repeating the findings of other commissions, and a lot of high
minded talk, all of it amounting to absolutely nothing in the way of pragmatic progress for women in the office and on the shop floor. Now that the real action on these longstanding concerns is dangerously imminent, the Opposition has once again resorted to type and we are faced with even more talk. This is not only unnecessary but, in the context of two decades of inequity buttressed by inaction, it is totally unconscionable.
Where women are concerned, employment inequity has been twofold, the inequity of opportunity to compete for certain positions and, within the positions they do occupy, inequity of salary-64 per cent of what men make for doing the same work, to be exact. As for inequity of opportunity, statistics show that despite the fact women now represent 41 per cent of the labour force and will reach 50 per cent by the end of the decade, only 4 per cent of senior managers and only 10 per cent of middle managers are women. Yet, in the face of this, we get weeks of stalling on innovative legislation that will require employers to integrate employment equity provisions in their long-range planning.
It should be stressed as well that the importance of the commitment expressed in Bill C-62, and the equity provisions of the Canadian Jobs Strategy Program, go beyond redressing long standing and obvious injustices. As we progress by real and practical steps towards employment equity, there will also be a spinoff effect that will be felt throughout the Canadian economy and Canadian life. As a nation we can no longer afford to exclude any group if we are to revive economically speaking. Be it women, native people, the disabled or members of visible minorities, the growth of the economic dimension these groups represent will stimulate the growth of the economy as a whole. Through the employment and training programs of the Canadian jobs strategy, particularly the job entry program, women are finally being given a chance to realize their goals within the modern workforce. Through important measures like this Bill we will ensure that women will encounter fairness and flexibility on the job as they strive to reach those goals.
This Bill is not a band-aid measure established in isolation from other Government programs and the realities of the market-place. On the contrary, it is designed to complement other federal initiatives to foster equity of opportunity and salary for Canadian women. Quite simply, women and other target groups must be assured of fairness of choice and fairness of income. This precedent-setting legislation is a practical step toward that goal.
I suspect that it is this very practicality which has caused such earnest confusion among the opposition Members. Some say Bill C-62 goes too far and some say it does not go far enough. Perhaps the source of their discomfort is that Bill C-62 actually presumes to do something and to do it in a reasonable, flexible framework which makes its goals achievable. No wonder the Opposition is disoriented. Can you believe, Mr. Speaker, no more studies, studies, studies; no more bureaucratic blizzards of paper work dumped on unsus-
November 18, 1985

pecting business people; no more inflexible regulations which break down the instant they are applied to regional or individual circumstances? What Bill C-62 proceeds from is the almost revolutionary presumption that results are more important than rhetoric.
We are making a clear commitment to employment equity and we are asking Canadian companies to make that same commitment. That commitment is backed by tough enforcement and penalty measures through the Canadian Human Rights Commission, although we hope to receive a level of co-operation which will make these enforcement measures largely unnecessary. The Government will also require contractors who do more than $200,000 worth of business with the Government to implement employment equity. And where Bill C-62 or other employment measures are concerned, we put these requirements into a workable framework. At a time when the Canadian economy is finally struggling, with the help of the Conservative Government, to get its head above water, it benefits no one, particularly women and other target groups, to throw employers an anchor of unattainable, unilateral and over-complicated legislation. A balance must be struck if the goals of equity are to be achieved. Make no mistake, Bill C-62 means business where equity is concerned. This Government is committed to equality for all Canadians and we are proud to be the first to go beyond the rhetoric of equality by taking concrete steps.
Bill C-62 ensures action and results. It also assumes good will on the part of Canadians as its legislative context. The advance interest and enthusiasm of Canadian enterprises, including some small businesses which do not even come under the legislation, indicates without question that this course is the right one.
The enthusiasm of participants, combined with the urgency of the situation for working women and other target groups in the labour force, makes the ongoing argument of the Opposition all the more empty, especially when we consider its track record on this issue.
We have made a legislative commitment to employment equity and we have backed it by real money and by objectives which are both fair and attainable. It is a commitment which is built upon the co-operation and initiative of all concerned. The time for talk is over. The time for action is now. Because it is so imperative that we move this issue forward in the interests of Canadian women, I am pleased to move, seconded by my colleague, the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Mr. Comeau):
That, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 9(4)(A), the House continue to sit through the lunch hour this day for the purpose of continuing consideration of the motion of the Minister of Employment and Immigration.

Mr. Speaker, we have just listened to the well practised rhetoric of the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) who eloquently defended what the Bill does not contain, that is, action. The Hon. Member said that the Bill means business. The Bill actually means that business has been heard far more clearly in its 80 per cent opposition to affirmative action than other voices. We have before us now a motion to limit debate on a little Bill that is such an inadequate response to so many of those voices. There has been the clear voice of the aboriginal peoples, of the disabled, of those with skins of a darker hue, and those of women. These voices have been recorded, reported, supported and ignored. These voices have told us that the most significant aspect of life is being able to have the same access to secure employment and decent salaries as everyone else in the country. These voices tell us that they ought to be able to house and clothe themselves and send their children to school on the basis of adequate income and access to jobs. It is an absolutely fundamental right of every person to have a job without regard to sex, skin colour, religion or anything else.
We have been told that it is no longer true that when members of minorities apply for jobs they are faced with a bigot who says: "Coloured people are not employed here". We have been told that complaints presented to the Human Rights Commission have become less and less effective as explicit discriminatory action no longer occurs with the frequency of the past. We have been told that systemic and institutional barriers to members of minorities and women for promotion must be attacked. I have indicated clearly how that must be done.
We do not have a Bill which in fact will implement affirmative action or employment equity. We have instead a Bill which says, "No more. We are going to count minorities and count them twice. We are going to find out which companies are naughty and which are nice". In this Bill there is a mechanism for ascertaining whether or not the statistics of employment of minorities, women and the disabled reflect the population in an area where they have equal access to jobs.
Affirmative action has a number of elements and everyone who has looked at the issue understands what those elements are. If we are going to have an adequate Bill, it should be directed at the entire federal sector and all government contractors. This Bill is limited in that regard. It says that affirmative action dictates that there should be a timetable. It says that affirmative action requires that there should be established goals and targets. The misunderstanding of that concept was clearly indicated by the Minister when she said that quotas become ceilings. That is the clue to the orientation of this Bill.
Affirmative action has been in existence for almost two decades on the North American continent. In places where affirmative action has been effectively implemented quotas have not been set. A quota is a nasty flag raised by those who oppose affirmative action. It elecits all types of negative

November 18, 1985
Time Allocation
responses. It is the bugbear of those who oppose affirmative action. The fact that the Minister herself refers to quotas in the context of affirmative action indicates the orientation of the Bill which is before us. As the previous speaker said, little is imposed upon business in the implementation of affirmative action. True affirmative action requires something more than counts; it requires targets, timetables and an enforcement mechanism. More important than anything else in order to be effective is the necessity for penalties. Affirmative action must be based on a plan or plans which are specific to the businesses involved in a situation which has to be addressed. That plan should also include employee or union involvement along with that of management and members from the designated groups. None of this is contained in the Bill before us. The Bill is a mockery-a mere sham-in response to the needs, concerns and actions requested by women, the disabled, natives and the visible minorities. It is no wonder that the Government is trying to impose a limitation on debate. What the Government is saying to those of us who sit on this side of the House who want to communicate the message that the designated groups would have us communicate is: "Shut up. We do not want to hear any more about it".
We have a little Bill which we intend to pass which ignores all of what has been said. We are purportedly leading the nation on a track of real progress in answer to discriminataion in employment. Yet, when we look south to the United States, which has a history of slavery and struggle in terms of the civil rights movement, a country to which we have compared ourselves and which we consider as being so much better in so many respects in terms of its treatment of women and minorities, we see affirmative action programs which are far more effective in the key areas. The Americans have requirements for timetables. They have targets and penalties which apply to all federally-regulated employers and all federal contracts.
The designated groups under this legislation have asked for contract compliance. Yet there is only limited contract compliance set out in the Bill. They have asked that the number of employees be reduced to 50, as it is in the United States. That has been denied. What we have before us is a betrayal of all of those whom this Bill purports to serve. It betrays the young native who says that violence and suicide is a common occurence on reservations where youth unemployment might be 100 per cent but is actually close to 90 per cent. There is a betrayal of the highly skilled female secretary who makes less than a janitor. It is a betrayal of the 70 per cent of black youth in Halifax who are struggling to find jobs. It is a betrayal of the disabled who were promised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that their needs for employment equity would be looked into and that action would be taken.
No wonder the Government wants to shut us up. It does not want to hear the message. It wants to get through with the matter quickly so that, presumably, no one will notice the magnitude of the betrayal of the needs of so many of the people in the country. It is a shame that the Government does not want to listen. It refuses to hear what has already been said so many times. Perhaps it is a waste of time to continue
the debate because for half a century the minorities have been asking for the type of action which affirmative action would provide in allowing them to have equal participation in our society. Maybe it is just as well that we be frank. The Government is not interested and it wants to cut off debate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in this important debate on Bill C-62 and on the motion of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald).
Women, the disabled and ethnic minorities have waited long enough for the type of practical and effective employment equity legislation which Bill C-62 represents. During debate on the Bill we have all heard of the frustrating statistics which demonstrate the need for employment equity legislation in the country. We have heard of discrimination in the workplace which visible minorities and the disabled experience almost every day. We have heard of the wage gap working women face simply because they are women. Above all, we have heard of the tremendous waste of human resource and talent that this type of discrimination wreaks on our country and upon our furture. The time to act is now. Further delay of the Bill will only delay equality in the workplace.
The question we on this side of the House are asking, is why would the Opposition want to delay legislation which will give millions of Canadians new hope and new opportunity? The country simply cannot wait. Why delay legislation which, for the first time, will give the Human Rights Commission the date and the resources it needs to further the cause of equality in the workplace? Why delay legislation which, for the first time, will compel hundreds of private firms which deal with the Government to implement workable employment equity? Above all, why delay legislation which will bring the country into the 21st century in terms of fairness and equality in the job market?
The Opposition would have us believe that the answer to employment equity lies in quotas and Government red tape. They simply do not understand that quotas are unworkable, unfair and unnecessary. A recent poll conducted by the American Enterprise Institute in the United States found that 77 per cent of blacks actually oppose quota-style affirmative action programs. Despite forced quotas, discrimination still exists in the U.S. because employers treat people as numbers and as fillers for Government forms. Our Government believes people should be judged on merit and capability.
Bill C-62 reaffirms our intention of encouraging a positive and progressive environment for employment equity in Canada. As the Minister of Employment and Immigration has said, employment equity is about opportunity, the opportunity for Canadians everywhere to earn a decent living and to participate fully in our society.
This past weekend the newly elected Leader of the Ontario Progressive Conservative Party, the Hon. Larry Grossman, highlighted the importance of involving ethnic minorities more actively in the political and decision-making process. I share his sentiments. I applaud his commitment to equality oppor-
November 18, 1985

tunities when a new Progressive Conservative Government is returned to the great Province of Ontario.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-62
speechtext:
Bill C-62 represents an important turning point for Canadians. It signals that Canadian women are not going to be balkanized in clerical and service sector occupations. It signals that native people and visible minorities are not going to be denied opportunity because of the colour of their skin. Job discrimination, whether overt or unintentional, can no longer be condoned by a country that expects top performance in its industrial sector. Systemic, unintentional discrimination is inefficient and a waste of our human resources and impedes the natural flow of the free market. Mr. Claude Bruneau, President and Chairman of the Imperial Life Assurance Company of Canada recently said, and I quote:
I see 50 per cent of the population becoming financially autonomous and scant attention has been paid by business.
He also said there was a great opportunity for women as business leaders. And this, I might add, would be of benefit to the whole country. This Government's vision of a fair and equitable labour market can truly serve the interests of all Canadians. Fairness and equity are more than mileposts for social justice. They also show that this society needs the participation and contribution of all our human resources if we are to be competitive.
We are taking a positive first step towards change, one which works with Canadians, not against them. By requiring the implementation of employment equity we are telling employers to take the time to examine the composition of their workforce. Are there barriers that block the entry of potentially good workers? Are these barriers truly necessary to the job? Does everyone have access to training? Who got promotions last year? Is there under-representation of women or native persons at the executive level, and if so, why?
Therefore, let me say that, in the interests of justice, prosperity, and basic human rights, this Parliament should pass Bill C-62 as quickly as possible and prove to Canadians our commitment to equality and social justice.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak once more about Bill C-62, which aims at promoting employment equity for women, visible minorities, the native people and the handicapped.
These objectives are quite valid and I support them wholeheartedly. However, I object to Bill C-62 as it now stands because it does not provide the mechanisms required to achieve the stated objectives of the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Like many pressure groups representing women and the three categories mentioned earlier and covered in Bill C-62, I believe that it is essential that legislation to promote employ-
Time Allocation
ment equity include effective enforcement mechanisms, target dates and penalties.
Since the tabling of Bill C-62 in this House, the Committee on Equality Rights has tabled its report. Earlier, I heard my colleague say that Bill C-62 should have the support of all Opposition Members. However, I am somewhat surprised at what she said because she herself supported the report on employment equity which deals among other matters with Bill C-62.
It has been said that the Conservative Government wants to apply Bill C-62 to all companies having more than 100 employees, but not to the Government itself in its capacity as an employer. Yet, Mr. Speaker, the recommendations contained in the report of the Parliamentary Committee on Equality Rights, of which my colleague was a member included recommendation No. 60, which states:
We recommend that employment equity legislation apply to all federal public sector employers and to employers under federal jurisdiction, with necessary adjustments being made by regulation for small businesses and agencies.
This was one of the recommendations of the Committee, but this Bill does not reflect these recommendations.
I also believe that the minorities should co-operate with employers and unions in developing employment programs. A great many groups representing women, the native people, the handicapped and visible minorities have deplored the lack of mechanisms to enforce employment equity programs. The Abella Report emphasized the importance of having an independent agency responsible for implementing employment equity programs. The report Equality for all also recommends that the legislation designed to guarantee employment equity contain implementation mechanisms through which the Canadian Human Rights Commission would develop special programs and have the financial and human resources it requires to do so. The members of the Parliamentary Committee on Equality Rights also thought that the employment equity legislation should provide for a periodical review of special programs so that they might be adjusted or cancelled according to how the situation develops.
I am somewhat surprised that the Hon. Member described this Bill as sensational this morning, as there is a striking contrast between this legislation and the report she signed herself. Since employment equity concerns not only the labour force, as stated in the report of the Parliamentary Committee on Equality Rights, but our whole social structure, the members of the Committee recommended a series of measures to help women, the handicapped, native people and visible minorities to achieve real equality. I therefore question the statements made by the Hon. Member earlier. Mr. Speaker, the recommendations of the Committee are important since the family responsibilities of women constitute real obstacles to their equality on the labour market. The same is true of the major financial costs which the handicapped must bear if they are to live a relatively normal life.

November 18, 1985
Time Allocation
Realizing the importance of these factors in the daily life of Canadian men and women, the Committee also recommended that, in consultation with the provinces, the Federal Government urgently take measures to ensure that day-care services in Canada be available at affordable prices. The Committee on Equality Rights, of which my colleague was a member, also wants the Income Tax Act to be amended so that the handicapped can be entitled to deduct from their income the costs of special devices and services, including additional job-related transportation costs which are a direct result of their handicap.
This report is one of the best that this House has received, and the Hon. Member who extolled the merits of Bill C-62 this morning was among those who signed it. Once again, I am somewhat confused about this because, in view of this report, Mr. Speaker, 1 am in fact urging the Minister of Employment and Immigration to withdraw her Bill on employment equity and introduce legislation which will better reflect the recommendations of the Parliamentary Committee on Equality Rights. This report was accepted by the three political parties, I think it is a progressive report, and I believe that the Conservative Government should take advantage of the fact that it was a unanimous report to implement new guidelines. The Minister of Employment and Immigration told reporters last week that the women's movement should deal with basic issues and put less important matters aside. In my opinion, she now has a golden opportunity to introduce in Bill C-62 elements which groups representing women, visible minorities, the handicapped and the native people consider essential. This bears repeating: I think that the report on equality rights ranks among the best we ever had, so I am surprised that the Minister would not implement the recommendations made by the committee members concerning this Bill. I am still more surprised to see my colleague support a Bill which is lacking, when in fact she belongs to the sub-committee which presented a report on equality. I find that quite astonishing.
Regarding the Bill under consideration, we learned last July that the Government would only require from employers a statement that they endorse the principle of equal opportunities for men and women, nothing more for the time being. It falls far short of the Abella report recommendation. The report went as far as urging that the Canadian organization responsible for ensuring compliance with equality provisions related to employment in the federally regulated sector monitor as well compliance with private sector contractual obligations. Well, this Bill C-62 does not provide for any such commitment. As I pointed out a few minutes ago, the lack of enforcement mechanisms makes the Bill under study totally useless.
Mr. Speaker, allow me to refresh your memory concerning the reaction of some politically independent people and groups who are strongly opposed to Bill C-62. At a meeting organized last spring by the federal caucus of Conservative women of the Montreal region, UQAM labour sociologist Evelyne Tardy stated that toothless employment equality legislation would be useless.
I have received a great many telephone calls from groups of women concerned about the Conservative Government's lack of political will in the area of employment. On the other hand, I have received a great many phone calls from groups of women and other people supporting the report of the Subcommittee on Equality Rights. 1 should like, therefore, my hon. friend to come clean. As I listened to her, 1 had the clear impression that she had two different ways to approach this bill.
Of course, I am very disappointed today that the Government should impose closure on such an important bill as this. This demonstrates the Conservative Government's lack of understanding of and sensitivity for women issues. We are all aware that in Canada poverty is a fact of life for a great many women and that today, in 1985, 42 per cent of married women with children must go out to work. I do not think that a bill such as this will make it possible for Canadian women to achieve the place they deserve on the labour market. I am extremely disappointed and I want to make it quite clear again that I categorically oppose Bill C-62 in its present form.
Mir. Rob Nicholson (Niagara Falls): Mr. Speaker, when I return to my riding of Niagara Falls on the weekends I am very pleased to discuss some of the federal issues which are before this House. One of the things that I am particularly proud and pleased to discuss are the provisions of Bill C-62, the employment equity Act. People like it. It appeals to their basic sense of fairness which, I think, characterizes Canadians.
When my constituents ask me about the progress of this Bill, I have to be fair about it. I tell them that the NDP and the Liberals are against it and are trying to hold it up, just as they are doing with several other pieces of legislation before this House. They argue that it does not go far enough, that it does not have enough enforcement to scare Canada's business community into action. They then issue their classic response: "Let's do nothing, let's forget about it and maybe the problem will go away on its own".
I am disappointed, Mr. Speaker, with that attitude. However, having observed the proceedings of the Thirty-third Parliament up to this point, I am not surprised by it. I believe it is that kind of closed-minded outlook that lies at the root of the need for this employment equity legislation. Canadians want strong, forceful legislation which appeals to positive rather than negative qualities. I think the Government has achieved this with Bill C-62, but the Opposition's response is just to keep talking about it and eventually forget about it. I think I know the reason for that. I think they are afraid that this legislation will be successful and, obviously, this is a risk which they would rather not take.
I will use a few minutes to explain why the Government's positive yet firm approach to employment equity is, in my
November 18, 1985

opinion, the best way to proceed. I ask you to think about people who are handicapped, many of whom, up until a few years ago, faced a life of isolation and institutionalization. Many of these individuals are now out in the community ready and willing to work. However, they are faced with a 50 per cent unemployment rate. 1 think that is most unfortunate because these people can and want to work. They do not want to sit at home collecting unemployment insurance cheques or disability pensions. Many of them have valuable skills. Many of them could fit in well as professional individuals. Others have top rate clerical or semi-professional skills. These individuals wake up every morning into a world of "can't do". Those "can'ts" are inspired by social barriers and implied restrictions.
Physically handicapped individuals have a tough time going door-to-door. Many times they cannot physically get through the employer's door. This is one area in this particularly difficult problem where I think we have made progress. It has been encouraging for me to note in recent years that changes in building codes require all public buildings to provide access ramps and other facilities for the handicapped. Even if that individual can get through the door, Mr. Speaker, he must still overcome the invisible barriers of prejudice and fear. This is another unfortunate aspect of this problem. However, many times when 1 have spoken with employers who have hired physically handicapped people I have noticed, almost without exception, that their efforts have been rewarded. However, Mr. Speaker, that is not enough. Where prejudice and fear remain there will continue to be a tremendous waste of potential.
1 believe that Bill C-62 will help to change this situation. No longer will employers be able to hide from the problem by denying its existence. They will now have to implement equity and demonstrate its implementation by reporting on the results. Now they will have to explain what they are doing about hiring disabled individuals as well as women, native people and members of visible minorities. However, 1 think it is important that the Government not lean over employers' shoulders and say that they must hire target groups whether or not they are qualified. There are no quotas here. Too often when quotas have been implemented they have represented a ceiling for the employment of minority groups. Rather, the data which employers must provide in their annual equity reports will provide a bench mark, a public comparison of employment equity performance. Consumers and Government agencies, for example, will know if a business is pulling its weight or is just sloughing off its responsibilities.
As Bill C-62 is aimed at larger businesses, often with a high public profile, a poor equity report is, at the very least, embarrassing. More important, the Human Rights Commission is now going to be able to look for evidence of discrimination and will be able to use its power to initiate investigations. No longer will reliance be placed solely on idividuals or groups to file complaints.
Why should only larger businesses with 100 or more employees be involved? Why rely on the Human Rights
Time Allocation
Commission to assess the report data and decide on enforcement under its human rights mandate? The answer is simple. Canadians hate bureaucracy, Mr. Speaker. 1 know that some of my friends in the Liberal and New Democratic Parties love bureaucracies, but 1 think most Canadians hate them. I hear some of my friends insisting that they probably invented bureaucracy. I am not going to quarrel with their interpretation of history.
In any case, Mr. Speaker, while adhering to the reporting requirement will cost larger firms less than $2 per employee, the administrative burden on smaller enterprises could be unreasonable and unworkable. Unlike my hon. friends beside me, we certainly do not want an army of equity police descending on Canada's employers. Nor do we want to spend more of our tax dollars on bureaucrats' salaries, when the money could be better used to create real jobs. Therefore, the message to the employers of this country is simple. Either clean up your act or we will be prepared to act further. Clean up your act and do it now.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has already indicated to the House that she will see to it that the Human Rights Commission will be provided with the additional resources to ensure that employment equity gets proper attention. Fortunately, the commission is already well equipped with administrative and staff resources to handle equity cases. It is a practical and efficient way to run the Government and meet the needs to target group members.
Let me conclude by making some basic observations. Our Government in the first in Canada's history to go beyond rhetoric and false promises. It goes beyong the bull-headed claims and stonewalling of the NDP and Liberals. It is the first Government to actually implement employment equity legislation.
It took courage to bring this Bill before Parliament. Many vested interests would prefer not to see it happen. My colleagues in the Liberal and New Democratic Parties are part of those interests who do not want to see it happen. However, for the disabled individuals, women, native people and members of visible minority groups, this Bill offers hope and promise. That promise is extended to all Canadians who will be able to learn what these individuals can do.
I think Bill C-62 is a courageous and exciting piece of legislation. It is an historic place of legislation and it is time that it became the law of the land.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-62
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the time has come to end the debate on second reading of Bill C-62, the legislation on employment equity, otherwise the public might start thinking that South Africa's philosophy has rubbed off on this Parliament.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, discriminatory measures, although usually not intentional, are preventing many members of target groups from enjoying the same advantages as other citizens with respect to recruitment, promotion and remuneration.
We must act to change this situation. We must take action to guarantee their rights: the rights of women, native peoples, the handicapped and members of minority groups. We must take action to ensure that women have equal access to jobs on the labour market.
We must take action for the benefit of native peoples, so that our position internationally with respect to various aboriginal peoples is not used against us and we are not made out to be hypocritical in the extreme.
We must act to help the handicapped, since during the International Year of the Handicapped, we recognized that they have the same rights and privileges as other citizens, and it is therefore essential to take appropriate action to guarantee those rights.
We must act to help members of visible minorities and ensure their full participation in the economic, social and cultural life of this country.
Mr. Speaker, it would therefore be in order to question the motives of some individuals and groups in criticizing this legislation. Some people claim that their hesitation in embracing the intent of this legislation is due to a lack of information, but this is hardly a convincing argument because of the abundant literature available on the subject.
I would like to add that that literature must be read with the requisite objectivity, because there will always be those whose minds are so narrow they will object to fundamental principles such as those that guide this Government.
Individuals or groups who object on economic grounds should be reminded that they are taking a very short view of the situation. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the amount to be spent on setting up equity measures is only a drop in the bucket, if we consider the amounts we would have to invest in the future to remedy a situation caused by our neglect. How many billions of dollars will have to be spent on assistance for women, native peoples, the handicapped and members of visible minorities if we do not give them the opportunity to become active participants in this country's economy?
Mr. Speaker, I am thinking of those who are using dilatory tactics to reduce the impact of this legislation or to get rid of it altogether. They will have to take the responsibility for their actions. It is intolerable that in a society that calls itself
Time Allocation
civilized, we should doom a very large part of the population to being second-class citizens or ignore their rights altogether.
And there are those who will claim that we are doing this for purely political purposes. That is not so. We could indeed have delayed our response to the Abella Report recommendations, saving it as icing for a cake for the end of our mandate. Quite the opposite, we wasted no time reacting to the proposals in that report, we introduced a legislative measure, Bill C-62.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, their objections do not hold. What is needed now is that we get out of our lethargy, get rid of our prejudices and act. I referred earlier to South Africa. I will now have a few word on the historical situation of our southern neighbours. After the war in the middle of the 19th century, many generations had to come and go before they could take corrective measures against discrimination. Fortunately, this country did not have to go through that kind of war.
However, because of our peaceful nature and situation, we came to think this was paradise. Regretful as it may be, paradise this is not. We have been practicing various forms of discrimination, more often than not in an unconcious, unintentional way. Some will say they have nothing to do with it, not being at the root of these problems, and not supporting them in any way. But this is a social problem, Mr. Speaker, and we are all involved. Whether by our awareness or through our decisions, we can and must act.
We can act, Mr. Speaker, and we, as a Government, have decided to introduce a bill that will be the starting point of a major movement at the national level to fill gaps that have been plaguing this country for too long, and which we can no longer tolerate.
As I mentioned in my opening remarks, Mr. Speaker, I feel the time has come to put an end to these discussions, otherwise we will be showing contempt for Canada's people and institutions.

We are debating a motion by the Government to limit debate with respect to Bill C-62 dealing with employment equity. When that Party was on this side of the House, time and time again it argued against closure. The Conservatives said it was undemocratic and that the Opposition should be given as much opportunity as possible within reason to debate a piece of legislation. They said it was wrong to cut debate and

have the guillotine fall. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) when she was in Opposition spoke out very vigorously on that subject matter. Now the same Minister today has moved the motion to cut off debate to stifle any further debate on Bill C-62.

I will try to answer that question in the few precious moments I have to speak today. It appears obvious to me-and I think it is obvious to Canadians-that the Government is embarrassed by Bill C-62. I am sure you are aware, Mr. Speaker, that in 1982, at a policy convention of the Conservative Party of Canada, 75 per cent of the delegates felt that women were not entitled to special employment programs. subtopic: SOUTH MORESBY-CONFRONTATION BETWEEN LOGGERS AND HAIDA INDIANS
SOUTH MORESBY-CONFRONTATION BETWEEN LOGGERS AND HAIDA INDIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thousands of miles to the west a major confrontation has emerged between the loggers and native Indians of South Moresby, particularly on Lyell Island. This region contains several areas of high ecological and anthropological importance. As well, the forest industry there provides jobs, local services, and a way of life to many citizens of my home province. It is my view, and the view of many of my constituents, that the best land use is an intelligent, multi-use approach which will meet the needs of many, as opposed to a single use concept which will favour the few.
The economy of our province needs every job we can hang on to, and jobs are definitely at stake in the South Moresby issue. Everyone involved agrees on one thing-there is no opposition to the creation of some sort of wilderness area or park over the vast majority of these islands; but the same people who would object strongly to the flooding of a portion of B.C. farmland see no problem in removing a portion of the allowable cut which provides hundres of jobs.
The Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) has advocated civil disobedience on this issue. The provincial Leader of the New Democratic Party has said that he is ashamed to be a British Columbian. I am proud to be a British Columbian. Those who live and work in the shadow of the tall timber do not view trees as two-by-fours with twigs. They respect the ecological balance of the forest. They have a right to share in that resource with all British Columbians.

EAST COAST-CALL FOR STATIONING OF HELICOPTERS

subtopic: MEETING BETWEEN UNITED STATES PRESIDENT AND SOVIET UNION GENERAL SECRETARY
MEETING BETWEEN UNITED STATES PRESIDENT AND SOVIET UNION GENERAL SECRETARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tomorrow the leaders of the two most powerful nations on earth meet in Geneva. I am sure I speak for all of us in this House, indeed for all Canadians, in wishing them well. There has been no meeting at the summit for six years. These have been six years of increasing danger, tension, and rising public fears. We can only welcome without reservation this vitally important summit and urge a continuation of such meetings on a regular basis.
Both President Reagan and Mr. Gorbachev have said that there is an urgent need both to prevent an arms race in space and end the arms race on earth. These must be Geneva's paramount goals. We have learned from a CBC poll that one-third of Canadians fear a nuclear war in the coming decade. Half of all Canadians recognize the nuclear arms race as the greatest threat to world peace and Canada's security.
Most Canadians have high hopes that this summit will improve superpower relations. These views are neither naive nor moralistic. They are opinions based on our history of active internationalism, problem solving, and opposition to nuclear proliferation. The Government of Canada should feel secure in the guarantee of public support for initiatives this country might take in easing tensions and ending the arms race. We do have a role in the sombre affairs of Geneva. It is our fate and our future that are at stake. Let us sincerely hope that the leaders will leave Geneva having taken a giant step back from the nuclear abyss.

Mr. Speaker, on November 18, 1918, Latvia became an independent democratic nation. Latvia lost that treasured status in 1940 when the Soviet Union occupied this small Baltic country.
