speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister for External Relations):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
subtopic: UNITED NATIONS EDUCATIONAL, SCIENTIFIC AND CULTURAL ORGANIZATION GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my speech today is to address Canada's policy on UNESCO.
First of all, however, let me express the shock and sadness with which Canadians heard last November 13 about the natural disaster in Colombia that resulted in the loss of so many lives.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has already addressed, on behalf of all Canadians, a message of sympathy to his Colombian counterpart, but I am sure that all Members of this House will want to join me in expressing once more our profound sympathy to the families of thousands of Colombians who died or have been reported missing as a result of this terrible disaster. I also wish to extend our condolences to the 50,000 Canadians of Colombian origin who may have lost relatives or friends as a result of this catastrophe.
Mr. Speaker, last Friday I announced that an initial contribution of $60,000 had been made by the Canadian Government to the UN Organization for emergency assistance and a donation of $100,000 to the League of Red Cross Associations and to the Pan American Health Organization. That same evening, a Canadian Forces Hercules aircraft left Ottawa carrying blankets, drinking water containers and emergency medical supplies requested by the Colombian authorities. We have also been able to send technicians with seismological equipment, who will back up experts on the spot responsible for monitoring developments in the volcano's seismic activity. Our embassy in Bogota is offering additional assistance and has also made its vehicles available to emergency relief teams.
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I met His Excellency Mr. Orlando Abello, the Colombian Ambassador to Canada, who advised me of his Government's assessment of the situation in

November 18, 1985
Statements by Ministers
this particular area of his country. After consulting with His Excellency, 1 would now like to announce the following additional Canadian contributions:
A contribution of $50,000 to World Vision;
A contribution of $60,000 to UNICEF emergency programs;
A contribution of $30,000 to the Canadian Catholic Organization for Development and Peace;
Funding up to a maximum of $100,000 for the Canadian Embassy in Colombia, to be spent on local emergency assistance projects.
I have also instructed my officials to report to me as soon as possible on potential opportunities for assistance.
In concluding this disgression, Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate our feelings of deepest sympathy for the people of Colombia during this time of grief following the worst volcanic eruption in 100 years.
Mr. Speaker, forty years ago, Canada was one of the co-founders of UNESCO. Why? Because for all Canadians, then as now, the objectives of UNESCO were and are of vital importance. UNESCO was created for the purpose of enhancing peace and security through exchanges among nations in the areas of education, science and culture. Peace in this world and the well-being of mankind were the goals that motivated the creation of the United Nations Organization and which are proclaimed in its Charter.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of my speech today is to reiterate on behalf of the Government of Canada our faith in UNESCO and our desire, following its Twenty-Third General Conference, to remain a member. UNESCO is playing a unique and invaluable role.
It would perhaps be useful to recall its basic mandate. In education, UNESCO combats illiteracy, trains teachers and teaching staff and also builds schools. It dedicates much of its efforts to promoting equal access to education for girls and women, the handicapped and the elderly, and to improving education in rural areas, an important and vital task that is also in line with the priorities of this Government.
In the area of science, UNESCO encourages scientific and technical development in all parts of the world. As a promoter of science, it supports thousands of projects in the world by helping others do the job instead of doing it itself.
UNESCO is also active in the fundamental area of culture, an area of great significance for the Canadian Government. The affirmation of cultural identity is a duty within the international community. We must learn to share our cultural resources. The steps taken by UNESCO to preserve historical sites in Venice, Athens and Carthage have been taken on behalf of the whole of mankind.
Finally, UNESCO has also been able to adapt to new realities. Mankind has entered the era of global communications. This is something which UNESCO, like Canada, was quick to recognize. I hope that all Canadian men and women are duly proud of the pioneer work carried out in this area by a Canadian, Mr. Marshall McLuhan. In 1983, together with Teleglobe Canada, the Canadian Commission for UNESCO created a prize bearing the name of this great thinker which is the highest distinction awarded in the area of communications.
As all can see from its many activites, UNESCO today is a modern and complex international organization.
Over the past 40 years, Mr. Speaker, the number of member states in the organization has increased from 28 to 160. A majority of the member states are developing countries. Many of them do not have the resources to establish permanent contact with an international network to exchange information and ideas on education, science and culture. According to our friends from developing countries, UNESCO greatly helps them preserve their cultural identity and opens for them large avenues of information. UNESCO was therefore right to direct a major part of its programs to Third World activities. In this regard, our support of UNESCO is an extension of our foreign aid program which is very much appreciated by the friends of Canada in the developing world.
Six weeks ago, UNESCO paid tribute to the Canadian Organization for Development through Education, an NGO which provides the farthest corners of the world with pencils, papers and books. I am pleased to report that this non-governmental organization has been supported by CIDA for a great many years. I am happy that UNESCO is there to recognize and encourage the work of organizations such as this.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that I have come back from Sofia determined to increase co-operation between the Canadian International Development Agency and UNESCO, for instance in the case of small projects which cost nearly nothing and which can have a great developmental value by promoting education, science and culture.
I emphasized earlier the benefits which accrue to developing countries thanks to their association with UNESCO; however, this does not mean that I underestimate the benefits received by industrialized nations through their involvement with this unique testing ground for new ideas. UNESCO is important not only because it allows a freer flow of information between nations, but also because it contributes directly to the development of knowledge in a world where we increasingly depend on each other economically, culturally, socially and politically. UNESCO has a stabilizing influence on the world because of the exchanges it allows. For instance, its publications make it the most important publisher in the world, and these publications reflect the values, aims and traditions of all societies. Such an activity is certainly irreplaceable.
November 18, 1985

Mr. Speaker, as we are all aware, UNESCO has had very serious problems in the last few years.
Canada has long maintained that 1985 would be a decisive year for UNESCO and that the 23rd General Conference in Sofia would be the most critical during this period. That conference has now ended, and 1 want to tell the House today that the Government of Canada is happy with its results. UNESCO comes out with a stronger commitment than ever to reform, and with the image of an organization that will live up to its responsibilities.
Having had the privilege of heading the Canadian delegation in Sofia, I was able to appraise myself of the good will and moderation shown by member states in the proceedings of that conference. Canada's desire for reform was broadly shared. Member states want UNESCO to work efficiently.
Why are we satisfied with the results? Because our reasonable expectations from that conference have been met, in every area where we had been asking improvements for the past year and a half.
What was the ill affecting the Organization to the point of jeopardizing its very survival?
The diagnosis made by Canada and many member states from all continents was the following:
UNESCO had to define more strictly its goals and priorities;
It had an urgent need to concentrate its activities and give up less essential programs;
It also had to review its financial, administrative and other
practices; and
It had to tone down its political debates.
Mr. Speaker, last spring, the executive council-within which Canada exercises its influence-laid the groundwork for a condensed and improved UNESCO program that met with the concerns I just referred to. That program, which resulted from very difficult compromises negotiated over the last year, was adapted to UNESCO's budget, a budget reduced following the United States' withdrawal in 1984. As Members in this House very well know, it is not always easy to operate within a budget that is reduced by 25 per cent. This, however, is what UNESCO has done.
That new departure may contribute in a very major way to the revitalization and refocussing of the essential programs for which the Organization was established. A more modest UNESCO must now double its efforts in order to win the confidence of sceptics over the next two years and beyond. To that end, vigilance will remain the order of the day.
To consolidate what has been gained, all members and especially the major contributing states will have to keep pressure on the Organization. In the long run, it is in the interests of the UN system as a whole to continue the reform experiment at UNESCO. Whether the necessary reforms are implemented will depend on whether we are prepared to persevere in our commitment to work from inside the Organization.
Statements by Ministers
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are interested in UNESCO. This interest is a sign of the tremendous goodwill organizations such as UNESCO enjoy among the general public. 1 am relying on the many non-governmental organizations and provincial and federal departments representing the various components of UNESCO's action in Canada to continue to support this work. I would especially ask the Canadian Commission for UNESCO to advise and assist the Government in this difficult task. I will do so because there may well be no other country in the world that is so conscious, at all levels of its society, of its international connections.
I said earlier that Canadians had a special relationship with UNESCO. I may add that UNESCO has a special relationship with Canada, as was shown by the many expressions of esteem I received in Sofia on behalf of our country.
Finally, I would like to recall at this point the Commonwealth's support for UNESCO, its goals and its dynamics of change. In Nassau, leaders of the Commonwealth countries emphasized the importance of renewal of international institutions in general. Following the same line of thought, the commissioners of a number of Commonwealth countries posted in London, including our own High Commissioner, wrote to Sir Geoffrey Howe, the Foreign Office Secretary, on Friday, November 15. They again mentioned the importance attached by the Commonwealth to Great Britain's participation in this very important international organization. They took this step because the Commonwealth countries realized that a great many of our educational, scientific and cultural institutions are historically rooted in Great Britain. UNESCO needs the wisdom of our British friends, as it does that of all nations.
Mr. Speaker, the results of the General Conference are clear, and we have considered them in the light of our position on the proposed reforms. The Government of Canada is very pleased with the progress already made by UNESCO in this respect. I can state quite positively that we shall continue to work within the Organization towards implementing the requisite reforms. We will not abandon ship. As the Prime Minister said not long ago: "We will not withdraw from UNESCO . . . We have asked for internal reform, and we believe that a start has been made. We want to achieve reform but from the inside."
In short, Mr. Speaker, by remaining within UNESCO, Canada intends to realize the vision of the Organization that its founders had when it was created. Mr. Speaker, if UNESCO did not exist, we would have to invent it.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS EDUCATIONAL, SCIENTIFIC AND CULTURAL ORGANIZATION GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Official Opposition and of our leader, the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner), 1 wish to express the shock and deep sorrow we all felt when we first heard about this great tragedy in Columbia. Along with the Government we extend our sincere sympathy to His Excellency Orlando Abello, the Columbian ambassador to Canada, and we ask him to convey our feelings to his Government and the people of Columbia.

November 18, 1985
Statements by Ministers
Within a few days, Mr. Speaker, almost two weeks in fact- November 7 as I recall-the Minister who has just spoken was telling us about another great tragedy which had occurred and the measures her Government would be taking to help the victims of that tragedy.
Then I pointed out to her that in a world . . . and what strikes me today in the two statements which I will attempt to link together is that when the two major world powers are about to meet in Geneva-I did say the two major world powers, for 1 never claimed that one was less powerful than the other-to seek ways to put an end to the mad arms race and, in fact, to unbelievable military expenditures while we know they are ready to attack one another at a moment's notice, as I said last November 7, we have yet to find mechanisms to bring quick relief to and defend people who suffer or become victims of disasters such as the one which has just happened in Columbia.
I made an offer to the Minister-and I still offer my humble assistance in such cases-either through parliamentary committee consideration or through non-government organizations with a view to finding ways of responding in an orderly manner to help people cope with major disasters, a world organization ready to intervene so as to demonstrate that we are determined to take action when tragedy strikes just as we are when it comes to military issues.
I would be remiss if I did not echo the Minister's remarks and extend sincere congratulations to our non-government organizations which are doing so much good, yet receive so little publicity. I am wondering whether such ministerial statements as we hear now and again might not be the ideal forum to come up with constructive propositions. In addition to these sums of money which I find quite small under the circumstances, I wonder if the time has not come for the Minister to consider the possibility of offering a so-called matching grant on top of the normal contribution of the federal government, the Government of Canada announcing its willingness to contribute one dollar for each dollar collected by non-governmental organizations whenever great disasters such as this occur. This would be a fine way for the Canadian Government and people to demonstrate their solidarity with the rest of mankind.
I hope that the Minister will contact her colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), so that following this and similar disasters . . . she indicated in her statement that some 50,000 Canadian men and women of Colombian descent are directly stricken. I wonder if we should not consider immediately the possibility of having young children, even though they have not been abandoned by their Columbian parents, to start new lives here, in Canada. I wonder if the Minister should not contact the Minister of Employment and Immigration to make it possible for these 50,000 Canadian men and women born in Columbia to sponsor a relative, a friend, or anybody else and help them to come to Canada. We should demonstrate our willingness and openmindedness through our immigration policies, and abandon certain requirements whenever such great disasters occur for the sake of demonstrating our solidarity with the rest of the
world. I am sure that if the Minister conveyed this wish to her colleague the Minister of Employment and Immigration, she would give a lot of attention to representations made not only by myself on behalf of my party, but by herself.
We have also heard upon this occasion an important announcement concerning Canada's intention to remain a member of UNESCO. It would clearly have been a disaster if Canada had announced today its intention to leave UNESCO.
I have read the statement very carefully, and it would be useful for the Canadian people to know-I always like the educational side of politics-about the background of statements made in this House. I must say that I received my copy in very good time. Someone else could have replied to it, but I have been asked to do so on behalf of my party. I have to say that this is a very cohesive and well written six-page statement, which must have required the participation of the entire Department, because many people are involved in preparing this type of statement. It is certainly not a waste of time to repeat to those who will be listening to us on television or on radio or who will read reports of our proceedings in the press how important we have always believed UNESCO to be.
In the field of education, how extraordinary is the fight against illiteracy. How exalting it is to train educational staff and to build schools. Is this a thankless task? Is this insignificant? We do not think so.
Making enormous efforts to promote equal access to education for girls and women seems natural in Canada and the Western World, but it is one of the major tasks of UNESCO, and this must be repeated and re-emphasized.
As concerns the handicapped and the aged, I shall always remember what I was told in my youth. My father, whom 1 often quote when speaking about such matters, told me that you can tell how civilized a society is by its attachment to its senior citizens and its handicapped.
I think that UNESCO is doing a marvelous job. In the field of science, as the Minister said so well, UNESCO promotes the development of science and technology.
UNESCO operates in the basic area of culture. As the Minister has told us, we are entering the era of global communications. Mr. Speaker, I shall not be long, but I must say that this Party, the Official Opposition, has always been and still is committed to supporting UNESCO, and I know there have been all kinds of debates within UNESCO, but as a political party we are sticking to that commitment.
The Minister today announced that Canada will finally remain a member and, I must thank her for that, because for a long while there were all kinds of rumours coming from all quarters. I did a little reading, in the little time at our disposal because I received the statement this morning. We have to work very hard and very fast. Somebody called from Montreal saying: "There is a statement by your friend that very distinguished Minister". So we had to get posted and 1
November 18, 1985

had read of course that there had been all kinds of discording notes concerning our support for UNESCO. I was concerned. But, finally, the Minister put an end to all those endless discussions. There were discussions in Paris, within the executive council, where doubts were expressed, doubts that may have stemmed from the fact that the United States were preparing to leave, as they in fact did. At that point, there is always a tendency to follow the same path, the same direction.
So the Minister said that we were staying. What must be emphasized, Mr. Speaker, is that for all those things 1 referred to, we have a budget this year, and Canadians must know that in the $8 million provided for-an increase of less than 1 per cent from last year's contribution-Canadians must know all the good that can be done with only $8 million. At the very same time that in Geneva certain people will again be shouting at each other, shaking world conscience, as to whether we should slow down or not that crazy arms race that is costing hundreds of billions of dollars, a major friendly country, a powerful friend, the United States, is reviewing its membership, and not only has it reviewed it, but has withdrawn from UNESCO although its contribution is hardly 8 times that of Canada in approximate terms. When we know how much good UNESCO can do, it is obvious, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister said in her statement that an organization whose member countries have increased in number from 28 to 160 in a few years, representing various visions of the world, very poor people, people who have been exploited, who have suffered from illiteracy, starvation and all the miseries caused by illness, the homeless . .. And all those people meet within UNESCO. However, one of the most powerful friends of Canada, our southern neighbour, decides to withdraw because it does not always get the upper hand in discussions. Indeed, it would like to make a scanty contribution when one considers all the good that can be done by UNESCO, and because it cannot convince its colleagues from 160 countries to come to its own conclusions, it withdraws.
I should like to ask the Minister if during the Sofia Conference where several Members of this House were present-I should add that we were invited but we were unable to accept-I wonder if Canada, this close friend of the United States ... I have to ask, as there is no reference thereto in the statement made by six countries . . . called upon the USA to return to UNESCO. I think that it is very important, because this new Government is proud of the fact that it maintains direct communications; a mere phone call. Call me Brian. Yes John. Yes, Ronny. Call me! 1 am listening. Did Canada play the role of a good friend and intermediary, the role of a country that understands tragedies and enjoys the respect of developed and underdeveloped countries.
And 1 wish the Minister or the Secretary of State or the Prime Minister would come back to us in two months and make the following important announcement: We have convinced the United States, in the interests of world peace and international co-operation, to renew its membership. That would be a brilliant coup for Canada. I would be the first to rise in the House and congratulate either the Prime Minister
Statements by Ministers
or the Minister for External Relations or the Secretary of State for External Affairs and say: Thanks to our discreet efforts, we have been able to persuade the United States to renew its membership. And thanks to our own membership, our ambassador did the same for the Commonwealth ... She said so in her statement on page 6.
1 wonder whether the same representations, coming from a close friend of the United States, were made to that country.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, may 1 say that at a time when the two superpowers are expected to meet tomorrow, today, I could not do otherwise but pray, because I am one of those people who believe that in these circumstances, one must meditate-meditation is prayer, after all-and wonder what the world would be like if tomorrow, those two superpowers who are meeting at last. . . just imagine, the world is terribly excited because the two superpowers are going to meet tomorrow. To me, it is the most natural thing in the world for the two leaders of the two most powerful nations on earth to meet. To me that is normal. The International Parliamentary Union, of which I was the president for Canada, expressed the hope many years ago that they would meet, without pre-conditions. And I hope the press will not ask them right after the meeting, as if they had to reach some kind of decision: What did you decide? To me, the fact that the two superpowers are meeting tomorrow is already a step in the right direction, even if they do not solve any problems. Seeing each other, looking at the intentions of the other side and going back home to think it over and coming back would already be tremendous progress.
Speaking of tremendous progress, that would certainly be the case if tomorrow, the two superpowers and especially the United States would realize that the best thing they could do for world peace would perhaps be to come back to UNESCO. And to pay their dues, after all, $64 to $70 million in US funds is not that much for the United States, if you consider the tremendous contribution it can make by being a member of this great institution.
So I thank the Minister for allaying the fears we might have had as a result of various statements which have been made. We know where we stand, Canada supports UNESCO.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, 1 want to join with all those who-and this is something we do not do often enough-wish to congratulate non-government organizations which do so much good, as I said, with little fanfare.
I cannot do other than conclude by saying that 1 am surprised the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney), the Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the competent Minister of International Relations (Mrs. Vezina) are not employing their time and their energies trying to convince the Americans, especially having such a close relationship with the United States of America, to return to the UNESCO fold. Look at all the good that UNESCO can do toward more understanding and sharing for such a small amount of money.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic Party, I am pleased to respond to the Minister's statements on Colombia and UNESCO. All of us admire the tremendous fortitude of the Colombian people in the face of this disaster and hope very much that our expression of concern will go to the Government from this corner of the House and to the people of Colombia.
Several years ago 1 served for almost two years on the committee of the House of Commons that was studying Canada's relations with Latin America. In the course of that study 1 had the opportunity to visit several countries in South America and became aware of the enormous courage of the Colombian people throughout their history. Not only did Colombia maintain a democratic form of Government at times when many, if not most, of its neighbours were succumbing to military and neo-fascist regimes, but Colombia took a lead in seeking democracy, stability and peace in Latin America. It continues to take that lead today through its work in Con-tadora.
At a time of enormous national suffering in Colombia, I am, as we all are, pleased that the Government of Canada responded immediately and is continuing to respond with financial and
other assistance. As the Minister has noted today, there will be further assistance through non-governmental organizations. It seems to be a very tiny response given the enormity of the problem. I hope the Government will be able to increase its contributions, not only in immediate emergency aid and particularly financial aid which are required by the people of Colombia, but also in further reconstruction efforts.
There have been many tragedies over the past year. There has been the famine in Ethiopia and the response of the Government, which was a good and strong one. However, we were told and still are told time and time again that it is longterm aid or long-term reconstruction that is needed in the case of Ethiopia and indeed in the case of many countries in Africa which have suffered enormous famine. Similarly, in the case of Mexico and now Colombia, we want to help in the reconstruction works. That is what Canadians want to help Colombians achieve. I feel confident that the Minister will want to see us do that.
Also I hope the Government will seriously address the need for reform of our international financial institutions and our international financial arrangements which place such a heavy burden on Colombia, on other Latin American countries and on many other countries in the world that are trying to deal with debt crises. The continuing debt crisis and the inadequacy of the response to the crisis by international financial institutions, while not as vivid or as horrifying as earthquakes and volcanoes, nevertheless, it seems to me, will inevitably bring comparable suffering, poverty and tragedy to the peoples of Latin America and of other countries who are suffering so deeply from the crushing burden of debt.
On UNESCO, I was pleased, as all of us in my Party were pleased, to note the Minister's warm commitment to the survival and work of UNESCO. Indeed, she made a commitment on her own behalf and on behalf of the whole Government. The Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) mentioned some rumours which had been floating around that Canada might not in fact give its full support to UNESCO. Indeed, I first heard rumours under the previous Government that we might not continue our moral and financial support to this incredibly valuable organization and, therefore, I was glad to see that there was no foundation under the present Government to those rumours. As the Minister has said-and I thought it was a point well taken-if no UNESCO existed, one would have to be invented.
Also I would like to know whether the Minister has had any success in persuading the United States to return to the organization. It made a substantial contribution to the organization. In withdrawing from it, it not only undermined UNESCO and everything UNESCO stands for but, in a sense, it undermined the United Nations itself. In this connection I should like to urge that Canada, now that it has firmly recommitted itself to UNESCO, equally firmly recommit itself to the United Nations charter and move to strengthen the United Nations itself as an integral and essential institution for maintaining world peace. Very urgent measures are needed
November 18, 1985

and must be taken, for example, to curb the growing militarism and the growing anarchy which we see throughout the world. There are many steps that Canada could take within the United Nations to help curb such militarism and anarchy. The United Nations Security Council and the Secretary General could be and should be given-and Canada should press that they be given it-more authority to help maintain world peace. subtopic: PETROLEUM AND GAS REVENUE TAX ACT INCOME TAX ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
that Bill C-82, An Act to amend the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act and the Income Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker, this is the second occasion on which I have come before the House to introduce changes to the
8550

November 18, 1985
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I am looking forward to this assignment with greater hope and enthusiasm than on the previous occasion.

Last year I was responsible for shepherding the PGRT legislation left in limbo by the previous Government. It was an embarrassment for two reasons, the first being that the legislation had been left on the back burner for too long. Some changes had been announced about 24 months earlier.
More significant still, however, it gave rise to confusion because it contained nothing more than a mish-mash of inadequate temporary solutions, whereas a major reform was needed.

The reason for my greater enthusiasm today is that only seven months after the signing of the Western Accord, the Government has now done the major surgery which will restore Canada's oil industry to good health.
On March 28, 1985, my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney), announced the Western Accord. This historic event marked the end of a decade of dispute between the federal Government and western provincial Governments concerning energy. It signalled the beginning of a new co-operative atmosphere between the federal and the provincial Governments. The amendments included in this Bill are a direct result of that Accord.
I will not take the valuable time of this House to repeat the adverse effects of the National Energy Program, in general, and the PGRT, in particular. I will, however, point out some of the most glaring negative aspects of this national embarrassment. The PGRT was first announced in October of 1980, just over five years ago. I quote from the National Energy Program document:
Initially the PGRT tax will be set at the rate of 8 per cent of net operative revenues.. . deductions such as those for exploration and development expenditures, capital cost allowances and interest will not be allowed. As oil and gas prices rise faster ... the rate of the tax will be reviewed.
This tax was an unprecedented attack on a single industry and single region of Canada. The prosperity of western Canada and its oil industry was simply too enticing for the previous administration and it set about a revenue grab of major proportions. The PGRT collected over $1 billion from the oil industry in 1981 with no deductions for reinvested amounts.
Is it any wonder, I ask Hon. Members of this House, that the oil industry went into a disastrous tail-spin? Is it any wonder that thousands of westerners in the oil industry lost their jobs and their homes? Is it any wonder that businesses servicing the oil industry began to fail? Eastern Canadians as well were not immune. All too often we forget the economic ties we have throughout this country. The PGRT not only hurt western Canada, it hurt the suppliers of steel and other products in Ontario and Quebec, it also hindered young engineers who graduated from our universities from working in the meaningful jobs in their chosen careers.
That was not enough for the previous Government in its crusade to squeeze all of the money out of western Canada. Not content with the damage done by an 8 per cent tax, barely one year later the PGRT rate was doubled to 16 per cent and yet another tax, the incremental oil revenue tax, was introduced as part of the PGRT Act. It is no credit to the former Government that this newest tax lasted only a few months before being indefinitely suspended. It was obvious to all that the industry was in failing health and a number of other steps were taken in a belated effort to repair the damage which the Government itself had caused.
In 1982, a temporary 1 per cent rate reduction for conventional oil was introduced, along with a new small producer credit. An increased resource allowance was introduced for synthetic oil production. In 1983, capital expenditures on enhanced oil recovery projects were allowed as deductions. These changes were an admission of the fundamentally unsound nature of a revenue tax in a capital intensive industry. However, these were band-aid solutions. They were unable to solve the problem which continued to get worse.
It was against this background that the Progressive Conservative Party promised a new and a fair energy deal for all Canadians. In 1984 we promised to remove the petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax. We also promised to dismantle the Byzantine system of oil-pricing controls. We promised to remove the discriminatory system of petroleum incentive payments. One year later we have accomplished all of those things.
I want the House to know that I recently held a pre-Budget consultation with members of the oil and gas industry. I want to share with all Hon. Members today the mood of optimism, the new sense of opportunity and the climate of confidence which now exists in the oil and gas sector. I was told that government policies, including the Western Accord, have brought significant changes to the economic arena. The Canadian petroleum and natural gas industry has emerged from a mantle of politically imposed nationalistic policies to a new era of economic opportunity.
The last six or seven months have seen great changes in the industry. The Western Accord, coupled with non-punitive tax measures, and the deregulation of gas prices have enabled the oil and gas industry to rev up its own engine and contribute in a meaningful way to the economic renewal of Canada. It is with pride and enthusiasm that I present today a Bill which will carry out the promises of the Western Accord to phase out the PGRT by December 1, 1988, and to repeal the incremental oil revenue tax.
I would now like to point out briefly the specifics of the legislation before the House. Clause 6 provides for the following statutory rates to be applied to conventional oil and gas production from the current level of 16 per cent: in 1986, 13.33 per cent; in 1987, 10.67 per cent; in 1988, 8 per cent; and in 1989, nil. Synthetic oil production will be subject to lower rates as follows: in 1986, 12 per cent; in 1987, 8 per cent; in 1988, 4 per cent; and in 1989, nil.
November 18, 1985

The regulations to the PGRT will continue to provide a resource allowance of 25 per cent for conventional oil and 50 per cent for synthetic oil. These resource allowances reduce the statutory rates to result in effective rates over the next three years of 10 per cent, 8 per cent and 6 per cent for conventional oil and of 6 per cent, 4 per cent and 2 per cent for synthetic oil.
The new legislation provided does more than reduce the tax rate over the next three years. To stimulate new activity immediately, Clause 4 allows a full tax exemption available for new wells drilled after March 31, 1985. In addition, enhanced oil recovery projects are provided with options that will result in a more favourable treatment during the remaining years of the PGRT. Enhanced oil recovery projects can opt to exempt their incremental production after March 31, 1985, and major new energy projects can also apply for an exemption from the PGRT.
Another important feature of this Bill is the introduction of a PGRT offset in Clause 7. A new mechanism will allow for 30 per cent of the value of new unused exploration and development deductions to be applied against the PGRT in order to assist companies that are unable to realize income tax savings from new exploration and development expenditures under the Income Tax Act. This measures will be of particular benefit to a number of smaller Canadian companies and that is why we are proud to be presenting this Bill. The taxpayer can eliminate PGRT otherwise payable if he has sufficient unused income tax deductions and the consequential changes to the Income Tax Act that are required to implement this offset are included in the Bill before the House.
A final new measure introduced is a $10,000 annual deduction for individuals starting with the 1986 tax year. This measure will remove the burden of filing returns from several thousand Canadians who have some amounts of royalty income from producing oil and gas wells. All of these measures have combined to produce a remarkable recovery in the oil industry and the economics of exploring for and developing new oil and gas supplies have improved significantly. The provincial Governments in a new spirit of co-operation with us have complemented these changes with policy initiatives of their own and the economic recovery has begun and is well under way. It is creating jobs not only in Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia but in all the provinces of the country including my own Province of Ontario.
The Bill before us truly marks the beginning of a new era, an era of restored economic vitality for the oil and gas industry, for the thousands and thousands of Canadians whose livelihoods depend directly and indirectly on the oil and gas industry and for western Canada. I commend this Bill to Hon. Members and I know they will embrace it with enthusiasm.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on this Bill, but unlike the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall), I do not exactly embrace it with enthusiasm although I appreciate her optimism. During the election campaign, we as a Party
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act indicated that we would review the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax and certainly it was our intention to do so. The Minister spoke of a revenue grab from industry. That is just not the case. What is evident at the present time is that there is a money grab from the consumer as a result of this Bill and as a result of the policies of the Government.
The Government is giving the energy sector to the large oil companies, not the Canadian oil companies but the foreign oil companies. The Government has made sure that the oil companies are flush and will be successful but the consumer and Canadian companies will suffer.
I would like to move away from the issue of the PGRT for a moment and mention one of the things that the PGRT did. With its revenues, we were at least able to have a Petroleum Incentives Program. This is a program which the Government has completely abandoned. As a result, exploration on the frontier lands including the offshore has plummeted and the economic future of the oil and gas sector in Atlantic Canada in particular is very bleak indeed. At this time last year, 10 rigs were drilling in Nova Scotia. There is presently one rig drilling there. I am afraid this is the trend that is being set in Atlantic Canada. Of course this is not the viewpoint the Minister of State for Finance or the Minister of Energy (Miss Carney) have been putting forth. They are saying that exploration will surge and that there will be a very promising economic picture in Atlantic Canada. However, that is not the case and that is certainly not what we are seeing at the present time.
As I mentioned earlier, Canadian companies are in a position very different from that of multinational companies. The tax credit that has been granted for exploration on the offshore will not be satisfactory for Canadian companies. That is, it will not be satisfactory if there is any exploration activity at all. Shortly after the offshore package was announced by the Government, Mobil Oil, which made the application to the National Energy Board for the bringing of the Venture Gas ashore from the coast of Nova Scotia, withdrew its rig from that very field leaving only one rig, that of Shell Canada, drilling off the coast of that province. It is a very, very serious situation. The spin-off effects that the offshore has created in Nova Scotia are completely dissipating. We are left with empty office buildings and with people who had jobs at this time last year and do not have them now. These people have very bleak futures in the oil and gas sector.
What exactly will this new tax credit do for Canadian companies? It is a 25 per cent tax grab and all companies are being treated equally as they were under the regulations first stipulated under the Western Accord. However, what does that do for Canadian companies? It does not allow Canadian companies to take advantage of this particular tax credit because it is not a tax credit to the extent that the benefit is passed along regardless of whether the company pays taxes or not. No, it can only be deducted from income tax payable. As a result, companies which have had difficulties but have taken the initiative to explore and have taken a chance on the country, Canadian companies that are making an investment in Canada and as a result are not in a tax-paying position,

November 18, 1985
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act
cannot take advantage of this tax break to the extent that will be necessary. They will be allowed a mere 10 per cent of the benefits as compared to the 80 per cent that they were allowed prior to this measure which in addition to their normal income tax write-offs would require them to pay at best 10 cents on the dollar. These companies that have bought equipment for the offshore and are involved in the offshore have now had the rug pulled out from underneath their feet.
It is a devastating blow to Canadian companies in the oil and gas sector. In fact, the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada met with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to talk about the problems some Canadian companies are having in the transition from the Petroleum Incentive Program to tax credits. Some firms are worried that they will not be able to meet drilling commitments before the grants expire and, therefore, could lose their entire investment to date. Husky-Bow Valley, which has just announced a major oil find off the coast of Newfoundland, says that its financial support system may have been pulled out from under it. This is after three long years of effort on the company's part.
Mr. Robert Blair, the Chairman of Husky Oil, says that the end of the Petroleum Incentive Program throws a wrench into Husky's efforts and that it wants to get help through this transition period. The company needs to be able to utilize the investment which it has made. It has explored heavily and invested a great deal in expensive equipment. It would be economically devastating to have this equipment lying idle if the offshore activity stops after the expiration of the Petroleum Incentive Program.
The new tax system means that instead of receiving $40 million in petroleum incentive grants for every $50 million it spends in the offshore it will now receive $4.5 million. Mr. Blair says that the new tax incentive system leaves companies which have already invested in exploration and otherwise at a disadvantage while advantages occur to those companies which have not been doing so. However, he says that enough goodwill exists in Ottawa that a solution will be found. That is whistling past the graveyard, if there was ever an example of that. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has stated that there will not be any change to the program at all. Yet, Mr. Blair and his company and other Canadian companies are being dragged along over needles. What can they do but go along and hope that the Government will do something on their behalf? Only the Government can change this very Draconian measure for Canadian companies. There is no need for Canadian companies to be at a disadvantage in the country. This is Canada and these are Canadian companies. They have invested heavily and with the best of intentions. Yet, they are now being put at very severe risk. A great many of them will be placed in economic jeopardy and will not be able to survive. Why not give these companies the advantage? Why not allow them to take this tax credit and utilize this 25 per cent even though they do not pay taxes? Why not allow them to use it as a credit per se which would give them a 25 per cent advantage regardless of their income tax positions? Why not allow these
companies to pass it along to their shareholders if they cannot utilize it themselves? There are various ways in which Canadian companies could be helped by the Government if the Government wished to do so.
The Offshore Trade Association of Nova Scotia said that an acceptable level of exploration could not be sustained under this new energy policy. What is really happening is that there are far too many rigs bidding farewell to Nova Scotia. Some nine years ago there was a great deal of activity. Last year there was also a great deal of activity. However, this year there is but one drilling rig drilling off the coast of the province. Even the ex-Premier of Alberta, Mr. Lougheed, told the energy investment conference in Calgary that Newfoundland may need special help to bring the Hibernia oilfield into production. The industry also says that special deals may be necessary to bring western heavy oil projects and Nova Scotian natural gas into production; but the Minister says she has no more money on the shelf. She says: "Ottawa gave at the office." She says that she gave the industry a multibillion dollar break on taxes so she does not have to do anything more to help the smaller Canadian companies or boost the economies of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland by showing some flexibility. This is counter-productive to an area of the country which sorely needs economic activity.
It is not only Atlantic Canada which will suffer. We can now see that the Minister and the Government are retrenching and withdrawing from promises which they made with respect to the heavy oil sector and the tarsands. I would like to quote one example in particular with respect to heavy oils concerning the Husky upgrade which was promised by the former Liberal Government. It was substantiated by the Government in power which recently decided it did not want to go forward with it. The Government decided it wanted nothing to do with equity. It thought it had enough green stamps in western Canada that it could cut back on this project, which is what it did. It was a purely political move. The Government thought it would not be noticed. It thought it could withdraw from this oasis of plenty which it has given the oil industry and that it could withdraw the commitment once again. It made a promise to a Canadian company which it had been relying upon for over a year since the Government took office. Yet, it says it is investigating. It is taking a long time to investigate this matter-and no answer has come up yet. Meanwhile, this company is hanging by its fingers waiting for an answer. The Government has put Husky Oil in a very difficult position as a result of this change of mind. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources says that by removing taxes such as the Petroleum and Gas Revenu Tax there is incentive enough to invest. However, it is certainly not incentive enough to invest in the frontier lands. Nor is it incentive enough to invest in the offshore. She said that this move will be good for the country. I will deal with other points such as Canadianization and security of supply later.
1 wish to touch upon what this move will do for the group which will benefit the most. I speak of the multinational oil companies which are investing in Canada. These companies
November 18, 1985

should see their profits rise by 160 per cent by the end of the decade. Denis Mote, an analyst for Maison Placements Canada Inc., predicted that producing oil and gas companies in Canada will have profits of $8.1 billion in 1989 compared with $3.1 billion in 1984. During the same period of time revenues should jump 37 per cent to $36.6 billion and cashflow should soar by 70 per cent to $14.5 billion. The largest single factor in the profit picture is the elimination of the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax which will increase profits by 75 per cent without any other factor whatsoever.
What has the Minister done for consumers? This is where 1 return to the money grab from the consumers. In the recently announced consumer gas rate agreement there was nothing for the consumers. Certainly the producers absorbed a 12 per cent increase which the distributors were granted. However, when one considers the fact that natural gas prices in the United States are expected to decline by 10 per cent in the next year, then this is of no benefit to the consumers of Canada compared with what they should receive. In fact, the consumers of the country had been paying a fair price for natural gas under the former Liberal Government; but as the price went down world-wide the Government decided that it would not pass along the benefit.
Then there is the question of revenue for the provinces concerned. Will there be compensation for the money lost as a result of this Government's new energy policies? Will there be compensation for the lack of economic activity? The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stated last December that the Government was going to do away with the back-in provision. This, of course, was done. However, the Government is very slow to say how it will compensate Nova Scotia and Newfoundland for their resulting losses. We still have no knowledge of what amendments the Government will put forward concerning the Canada-Nova Scotia agreement or when they will be made known. As far as anyone knows there has been no dialogue on this matter. The Nova Scotia Minister of Energy is a man dangling from a 12-story window with little choice but to go along with whatever the Government offers. Purely and simply, the federal Government has hung the Province of Nova Scotia out to dry. That province has been left in a very precarious position and the federal Government is doing nothing to alleviate that situation.
So far as Newfoundland is concerned, there is a very good deposit of oil in Hibernia. As well, the recent discovery by Husky-Bow Valley increases the encouraging feelings we all have as to the future of Hibernia. However, the reduction in the world price of oil has left us somewhat concerned over what Newfoundland will receive from all this. The province has lost the back-in provision but has been told it will receive the royalties. Does that mean Newfoundland will have to wait until the world price of oil goes up before the companies actually start production? If so, what is in it for Newfoundland? Is the federal Government going to assure that province that regardless of the low price of oil it will receive some benefit from these changes? Of course, the economic stimulus
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act resulting from the development of Hibernia will be very important. However, will the oil companies say they are going to leave the oil where it is until the world price goes up? In that case, would the federal Government sit back and allow this to happen as it did with Nova Scotia? If so, production in Hibernia will certainly not start by the target date of 1992. It will be many years after that before we see any oil production in Hibernia unless this Government is prepared to take positive steps and become a factor in encouraging production as soon as possible. It is hoped, of course, that that will happen hand in hand with meaningful changes to offshore drilling practices to ensure the safety of those working on the rigs. The Minister has said that most of the royal commission recommendations were put in place, but we know that the most glaring deficiencies have not been corrected and that the men working on the rigs are still subject to very grave and unnecessary personal risk.
Where does all this leave us with respect to this Government's policies? What is the Government doing? I agree that we certainly have to stimulate oil and gas production and I am very pleased that western Canada is now selling increased amounts of oil. We hope their gas sales will increase as well. However, where does that leave Canada? Where is this Government's commitment to security of supply? By the turn of the century most of the oil and gas production will be controlled by OPEC or communist countries. We will then be in the position we were in in 1970 of being dependent upon the OPEC countries once again. What are we going to do to counteract that? What are we going to do to safeguard our security of supply? This is very important and we have to consider it. If we do not develop the offshore and frontier oil and gas reserves, if we do not make sure that the tar sands and the heavy oil reserves are brought forward when we need them, then we will be in a very difficult position. Our readily accessible oil and gas will be sold to the U.S. and our reserves will have been seriously diminished.
The Conservatives say that their energy policy is based on five goals. The first goal is that of a stable policy framework in which energy resources can support growth for the benefit of all Canadians.

This whole thing is getting out of hand. It is ironic, to say the least, that the multinational oil companies will always increase their prices within one day of each other and in the same amount. The consumer is being ignored. Security of supply is being ignored. Canadian oil and gas will be sold in the U.S. at a lower price than it is sold to Canadians. It is only a matter of time before that is going to become evident. It is fine to sell oil and gas in the United States. The producers must have a market for their products. That is a tremendously important feature.
I hope that the Government will remember its promises, Mr. Speaker. A few short months ago when we were debating the Canadian Oil Substitution Program and the Canadian Home Insulation Program, the Parliamentary Secretary told us in the House that it was not necessary to give people financial incentives to reduce the amount of energy consumption in their homes but that it would be done on a voluntary basis. We were told that there would be a program put forward by the Government which would promote conservation. It was proven in that debate that of all the energy money spent in the country the best value per dollar is in conservation. There is nothing even close to the value we get for conservation in the energy field. Yet, there has been no program put in place by the Government to deal with conservation. There has been nothing to substitute for that. All the Government wanted to do was to institute a money grab at the expense of the Canadian consumer and taxpayer. Any promise or commitment by the Government was thrown to the wind after the Government got its way with the Canadian consumer.
I think the Canadian consumer is becoming very jaundiced in its opinion of the Government as is indicated by all we are seeing in the press and all we are hearing from our constituents. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to stand on behalf of the New Democratic Party and debate this Bill today. I have heard the speech of the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) and of my colleague, the Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan), the Liberal energy critic. I will try to deal with some different matters, although there will be some overlap.
This is an important debate although one would not know that from looking around. That fact could easily be lost in the statistics, facts and terms that will be used. Generally critics are saying that the Government has not really done very much in most areas, but they have applauded the Government for what it has done in the energy sector. I acknowledge that. I think the critics are dead wrong. In my remarks I will try to explain why I think they are wrong. I think we have an energy crisis in the making. It is just a question of time.
This Bill specifically deals with the abandonment over the next five years of the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax. The PGRT, as it is known, was Ottawa's most effective instrument for taxing petroleum companies which have been masters of tax loopholes. This tax worked. It raised a lot of money for the federal Government. It was not liked by the oil industry. Handing over the proceeds of the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax to the oil companies, more than $2.4 billion a year, is supposed to encourage investment by the industry. This is the argument of the Government. It says it is giving all this money back to the industry to spur investment and create jobs. I believe that it is unlikely to do this because the real barrier to investment is the falling price of international oil and the glut of petroleum on the world market.
I think the real impact of this Bill, of the Government's energy policy, and of the Western Accord will be increased taxes for consumers, as my friend the Liberal energy critic, has just said. I think it will also mean cut-backs in social services in other areas because the Government is going to be starved for the money it has given to the big oil companies. I think it will also mean an end to the efforts to Canadianize one of the most important industries in Canada which has always been dominated by foreign-owned and foreign-controlled companies. One of the reasons for the National Energy Program and the motive for Canadianization was that between 1975 and 1979 foreign-owned oil companies were responsible for an outflow of $3.7 billion to their American parents. That is going to continue and it is going to increase in spades.
There is a double standard here, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the money that has been given to the oil companies. The double standard is that the federal Government's deficit is no problem when it comes to handing out money to the oil companies, but it is a problem when it comes to social programs for ordinary Canadians. At the same time as the Government gives, by its own figures, something like $5.5 billion in foregone tax revenues under the PGRT, it will have to recoup those revenues somewhere. Guess who pays. Ordinary Canadians pay. We saw evidence of that already when the Government tried to cut back on the indexation of the seniors' pensions. Only a mounted lobby by the seniors stopped
November 18, 1985

that from happening. We see evidence of that now in the Government's efforts to deindex family allowances. So you have a system where-
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the ordinary Canadian is the one who has to pay for this energy policy of the Progressive Conservative Government.
And the major oil companies will receive $5.5 billion by 1990.

It is a double standard, Mr. Speaker.
I would like to give some of these figures. In the first six months of 1984 the profits went up 40 per cent over those in the same period in 1983. Those are the figures of the Petroleum Monitoring Association. There was a 22.7 per cent increase in energy industry profits in the last 12 months over the previous 12-month period. That was reported in The Globe and Mail of May 16, 1985. Of those companies which made profits, the four largest oil companies in Canada, Imperial, Shell, Gulf, and Texaco, increased their profits for the first quarter in 1985 by 24.8 per cent. That was before the Western Accord and before this Bill. The oil industry was already recovering before it received this immense giveaway. Now, with the removal of the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax, large profits will accrue to the oil industry with a loss of revenue to the federal Government. It is estimated that with the stepping down of the PGRT under the Western Accord, $5.26 billion will be lost to the federal treasury by the end of 1989. Peters and Company, a Calgary energy analyst house, has projected that in 1986, the loss to the federal treasury will be $430 million; $680 million in 1987; $1.36 billion in 1988; $2.79 billion in 1989 for a total of $5.26 billion by 1990. Therefore, a rich industry is receiving more money. In addition, the price of oil was deregulated in April and went to world oil prices. As a result, the various companies made money. The price of oil found before 1979 was $29.75 a barrel. The price rose to the international level which was $37 a barrel at that time. Although new oil decreased in price, the increase in price for old oil was a windfall to those producers. Who got the windfall?
