speechtext:
I will come to that in a minute. Some 60 per cent to 70 per cent of the production by each of the major integrated oil companies was in old oil.
Imperial Oil and Texaco, both foreign owned, are this nation's largest oil producers. According to The Financial Post these companies will receive at least $50 million of additional revenue each year as a result of decontrol. The phase-out of the PGRT will result in a saving to these two companies of approximately $30 million in 1986, up to $150 million in 1989 when the tax is completely eliminated. The Minister of State for Finance did not say today that the two big winners, in addition to receiving the windfall as a result of going to world
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act oil prices, will now receive a tax break with the elimination of the PGRT. That is not to say that these companies do not pay taxes. They are supposed to pay taxes but those companies are experts at working their books in terms of paying taxes.
John Ferguson of Southam News states:
How can any government justify increasing sales and income taxes, higher gasoline prices and cuts in the indexing of family allowances-all in the name of spending restraint-while pumping billions out the back door to clever corporations with smart accountants?
I challenge the Government to deny those facts. According to the Government's figures, it will lose $5.5 billion by 1990 as a result of this change within the legislation we are debating today. According to Peters and Company Calgary, this figure is $5.26 billion.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) stated in the House of Commons that in the first year, the figure would be approximately $800 million. Furthermore, the western provinces agreed in the Western Accord not to take more royalties. In return for this system of vast giveaways to the oil industry, the Government gets a promise to create more jobs. There is no doubt that some jobs will be created.
This capital intensive industry has indicated that 300,000 jobs will be created. That figure is from the brief of the Canadian Petroleum Association and is used as part of the propaganda we see on television daily in the form of a progress report from the Canadian Petroleum Association. They have progressed by managing to reverse the entire energy policy of Canada and revert to an old system which existed before the first oil crisis in 1973.
My hon. friend, the energy critic from the Liberal Party, dealt with the effects on the East Coast as a result of this policy. While we will see some increased exploration and production in the offshore because the PIP grants are being phased out, we will see a system in which the multinational oil companies will dominate frontier exploration at the expense of the small Canadian companies which had a chance under the old National Energy Program. They will no longer be layers in these fields.
I recently read an article about Joe Mercier, who runs a small oil company in Alberta. It said:
Energy Minister Carney didn't know what she was doing, giving away the store. The oil industry did a great job with several years of full-page newspaper ads, containing all the catch phrases that Carney used-engine of growth, market-oriented prices and end discriminatory taxes.
This was stated by an oil man. He said:
Small and medium-size Canadian companies do the lion's share of drilling in Western Canada, thanks in part to federal government exploration grants to be phased out under the new energy deal.
He gave an example:
-in 1984, smallish Universal, had revenues of $25 million and spent $15 million drilling 103 wells.
By contrast, TexacoCanada Inc.-200 times larger than Universal-spent only ten times as much on exploration, drilling 53 wells in 1984 at a cost of $161 million.
Texaco Canada also handed out $156 million in cash dividends to shareholders-92 per cent of which went to its U.S. parent, Texaco Inc. of New York.

November 18, 1985
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act
And another $500 million flowed to its parent to "buy" a Canadian subsidiary Texaco Inc. already owned.
The Government has given the biggest windfall to Texaco, which is perhaps the worst spender in the oil patch. Imperial, while a better spender, will also receive a windfall.
The consumers are the ones who will suffer. They are beginning to realize this because I am beginning to receive letters concerning the increase in gasoline prices. I recently visited Saint-Jean, Quebec.

I was in Saint-Jean the other day, Mr. Speaker, and it was 60 cents a litre, while a litre of gas now costs 57 cents in Vancouver, British Columbia.

What we are seeing is increased prices for consumers.
I suggest that a matter which has gone unnoticed in the press and in the House of Commons throughout this debate concerns the fact that the basic issue in an energy program for Canada is the split of the energy pie between the federal Government, the provincial Government and the industry. A basic reason why the National Energy Program was developed in 1980 was that the federal Government was receiving virtually no money from the oil patch while giving more money in tax advantages and tax breaks.
I have written to the new Deputy Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to obtain a breakdown of the energy revenue between the federal Government, provincial Government and the industry under the Western Accord. I am told that these records are no longer kept and that the figures are speculative. While I criticised Marc Lalonde in this House many times, he always provided the figures. We are unable to obtain those figures from the present Government. That is a serious problem. As I suspect, the Government will be very short of revenues. I see the chairman of the Finance Committee in the House. I hope he will speak in this debate. If you give away $5.6 billion how do you recoup? What an immense gamble it is that the industry will create jobs and pay a lot more taxes without any control over it. We are dealing largely with a foreign industry that could send that money out of the country in dividends. How can you give a guarantee at a time when oil prices are falling? It is an immense gamble. It will not work and we will suffer.
I want to say a few words why I think there is a future energy crisis in the making. Canada is blessed with all the energy sources known to humankind. Canada is actually energy self-sufficient right now even in crude oil. We export one-third of our production of crude oil and one-quarter of our natural gas. We are back into the old system before the 1970 oil crisis of exporting to beat hell, if I might put it that way. It will cost us in the future.
When you look at the Western Accord you will see that it deregulates the price of oil. It gives massive windfalls and tax breaks to the oil companies and it substantially weakens the
control of exports of oil and gas. I draw Hon. Members' attention to an article in the Ottawa Citizen for Saturday, November 2, 1985 written by Les Whittington. It is a very perceptive article. Mr. Whittington quotes the opening words of the National Energy Program:
This is a set of national decisions by the Government of Canada.
The National Energy Program did not work as Mr. Whittington says. He said the program was hurt by the downturn in oil company activity in the western provinces, the fierce defence of provincial resource rights mounted by Alberta, criticism from the United States and the well-heeled oil lobby, and the scandalous air of wasteful spending associated with the NEP's generous exploration grants. As well there was the price miscalculation that oil would go up to $80 a barrel, which never happened and which really ended the National Energy Program. Notice the opening words of the National Energy Program: "This is a set of national decisions by the Government of Canada".
We now have an energy policy that is made by the oil industry, largely in New York of in the provinces. That is the difference between the National Energy Program and the program we have now.
The National Energy Program did make Petro-Canada into one of the largest gasoline retailers and refiners in the country. It expanded Canadian ownership of the industry from 28 per cent to 47 per cent. It turned up the reserves in Hibernia and Venture. It had those positive aspects but it had negative aspects as well. What we have done, to quote Mr. Whittington, is:
-passed the economic levers over to the companies with no way to guarantee results other than vague threats of renewed high taxes.
That is the gamble of which I was speaking and that is what we have done. In Mr. Whittington's words we have returned to a situation in many ways closer to what existed prior to the energy crisis that erupted in 1973.
Let me talk a little bit about that crisis, Mr. Speaker. There are many issues in energy, nuclear, hydro, conservation, alternate fuels, to name only a few. In my view the key energy issue, and it has always been key, is the level of our oil reserves and consequently the pace of our oil exports. Gas and oil are non-renewable resources. We are rapidly depleting the light sweet crude oil in Canada's western sedimentary basin despite a more than 1,000 per cent increase in wellhead prices from $3 to $38 a barrel.
Our accessible conventional crude oil reserves have gone steadily downhill since 1969 and they are still going down. This year we are exporting, as I said, about 30 per cent to 33 per cent of our domestic oil production. The world is now burning its oil at a rate of 900 billion gallons a year. One-fourth of the recoverable oil that existed when the first well was drilled just over a century ago has been burned. Exploration has already found about two-thirds of the oil it is likely ever to discover. At the present rate of consumption, there is roughly a 60 year supply remaining of world oil. The United States, which consumes one-fourth of the world's oil produc-
November 18, 1985

tion and which has only one-tenth of its oil reserves will look increasingly for its oil supplies, my friend was saying, to the Persian Gulf where what is left of the world's oil will be increasingly concentrated. You know the security problems there, Mr. Speaker. As we in Canada deplete our conventional oil resources, we will have to go further into the tar sands, the heavy oil, the Beaufort Sea and Hibernia. That oil will be more expensive to produce and it will cost consumers more money. Ordinary Canadian consumers will once again pay dearly. Geoffrey Edge, the retiring Chairman of the National Energy Board has forecast:
An increase in oil prices in real terms in the 1990s.
The National Energy Board has forecast that Canada will rely on the tar sands and the frontiers for more than two-thirds of its oil by the end of the century. Yet the oil companies still follow a consistent pattern. They want to export to get more cash. That is why they want to get rid of the Petroleum Gas Revenue Tax. They want more cash to pay for further exploration. Once they find the oil, they push and lobby to export it. There is big money to be made largely by foreign companies and they make a big buck, about $4 billion a year in natural gas alone. Canada is now the second most important oil supplier to the United States.
Tommy Douglas, when he was the NDP energy critic, once said that while a person can be forgiven one mistake, it takes a fool to make the same mistake twice. That applies to a country too, but that is what Canada is doing.
The Western Accord, as it is embodies in this Bill before Parliament, is a repeat of the mistakes of the 1960s and early 1970s. Quick exploitation of non-renewable resources, supported by tax breaks and other incentives, exported at fire sale prices to make a quick buck for largely foreign corporations is what Conservative energy policy is. That is going to cause us trouble in the future.
I have already talked about the winners and the losers in terms of deregulation. I have talked about the Petroleum Gas Revenue Tax and why it was disliked by the oil industry because it was so effective in capturing revenue from that industry.
I have already said how much money the federal Government would lose. John Helliwell, a UBC economist, concluded that following deregulation, the rate of return in the oil industry would be well above, and I say this to the Parliamentary Secretary, average even without the deregulation and the end of the Petroleum Gas Revenue Tax.
This is an industry whose profits are already up. We are already paying more money at the gas pump. We are paying 2 cents a litre more as a result of the Western Accord. Another 1 cent a litre is going on effective January, 1986. We are paying on the pretext of paying for the indexation of Old Age Security.
What we should have instead of paying 1 cent a litre at the gas pump is a windfall profits tax on the oil industry. We should have tailored the PGRT, and I say this to the Member for Calgary, so that smaller Canadian companies could get
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act exemptions and tax breaks making the big majors pay the taxes. Instead we are going with a policy that is in the opposite direction. I want to see jobs in the oil patch too but I want to see it done through small Canadian companies which, to my mind, are the best investors.
The Minister said in this House that the Western Accord will be the engine of economic growth and there will be up to 300,000 jobs. From where does that figure come? The phrase the engine of economic growth comes from the Canadian Petroleum Association, the lobby group for big oil. It comes from a brief to the Senate committee submitted by the Association in April, 1984. I wanted to quote the President of the Canadian Petroleum Association, but I do not seem to be able to find it. Basically, he was surprised at how much money the industry was able to get from the Government. As a matter of fact, he was shocked that it got everything it pretty well wanted.
Where is the evidence of job creation? I filed an application under the Freedom of Information Act and tried to find out whether the Department had studies. One would think that if $5.6 billion was to be given to the oil industry by 1990, there would be some studies on how many jobs would be created. One would think that they would not take the word of the Canadian Petroleum Association. It would be like Little Red Riding Hood taking the word of the wolf that she would be safe-"You are fine, little Red Riding Hood", says the wolf at the door. One would think that the Department would have some studies, but I found out that there were no such studies. In fact, the Department indicated that it had a compilation of other people's studies but noted that the prediction of the number of jobs to be created were based on "outdated and possibly unrealistic assumptions".
What kind of policy is it other than just a giveaway? Indeed, we have returned to the bad old days which saw us so unprepared for the last energy crisis. That is simply not good enough for the 1990s. This is why I think we will face another energy crisis, and that is why this policy has the seeds of the making of a crisis.
Disregarding present market price fluctuations, I believe we are seeing the underlying patterns like those which led to the 1973-74 crisis, the first OPEC crisis, and the 1979-80 prices. That is why we had a recession in Canada. The increase in prices was the source of much of our trouble and the great suffering of our people in the recession of 1981-82. In my view we do not have to vacillate between panic and complacency. We do not have to be manipulated by the big oil industry. We can do better. We must have security of supply. We must end our need to import oil in the future. We cannot continue to export a third of our production of sweet crude oil.
In the view of the New Democratic Party, the vehicle for doing this is significant Canadian ownership-public, private and co-operative. We can use our abundance of energy resources-and as I started my speech by saying, we have every one known to mankind-to give us economic growth and

November 18, 1985
Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act to make us the richest country in the world. It will add to national unity by opening up the North, the frontiers, the East Coast and the tar sands. We should not export it for a quick buck. We should not return to the pre-1970 policy which failed in the past and did not pass the muster when it came to an energy crisis.
That is what the Bill is about. This is one of the most important debates we will have this year in Parliament, and it was a privilege to be able to speak in it.

I was very interested in the comments of my two colleagues with whom I work fairly closely, the energy critics for the
Liberal Party and for the New Democratic Party. I will come to their particular arguments a little later in my discourse. There are a few points I should like to make before I deal with what they had to say. Suffice it to say, if I can just make a passing comment before I make my prepared remarks-

speechtext:
I will be nice. I found both speeches to be very interesting but very contradictory. They contradicted themselves many, many times during their addresses. 1 will try to cover that a little later in my remarks.
During the last general election, the Progressive Conservative Party made a commitment to the people of Canada to rid ourselves of the highly controversial and divisive National Energy Program introduced by the previous Government, a program which robbed Canadians of opportunities and very seriously impaired the economic and energy potential of Canada. My Party has always supported the goals of the National Energy Program. I think everyone in the country supports those goals of opportunity, fairness and energy security. However, we adamantly opposed the measures of the National Energy Program by which these goals were sought and the manner in which it discriminated against the regions of the country.
Canadians were presented with a choice on energy policy a year ago last summer. They voted for a new approach. I campaigned on it in my riding of Brampton-Georgetown. 1 know my colleagues from Ontario, Quebec and right across the country campaigned on a change to the National Energy Program. Canadians responded in spades; they voted for an end to the National Energy Program.
During our first year in office, we worked hard to fulfil our promise to change Canada's energy policy. The Bill before the House today represents but one element of a new energy policy for Canada. These new energy initiatives have become a reality through the Western and Atlantic Accords and then, more recently, through the frontier energy policy statement and the agreement on natural gas prices and markets. These energy initiatives have truly marked the end of the National Energy Program and ensured a replacement by a fair, non-discriminatory and constructive energy policy.
In establishing a new energy policy for Canada, it was most critical to get the Canadian petroleum industry back on its feet again. We wanted to return the industry to the days before the National Energy Program, to the days when the Canadian petroleum industry was a major source for investment in job creation, to the days when this industry was clearly the engine of economic growth for Canada. It should not be a dirty word in this country. Profits rely less on Government hand-outs and intervention. More opportunities are provided in the marketplace, and we recognize bottom-line profits as the basis for assessing taxes. The failure to recognize profits was clearly one of the major shortcomings of the PGRT tax.

I would like to give a brief history of this tax if I might, just to put the Bill in its proper perspective. The PGRT was introduced in the National Energy Program effective January 1, 1981, at an 8 per cent level. After only one year, the rate was doubled to 16 per cent, although many taxpayers were given a resource allowance of 25 per cent so that they paid an effective tax rate of 12 per cent on their net operating revenues. This represented a 50 per cent increase in one year. I suppose it is fair to say that the PGRT became the single most unpopular tax of all of those taxes introduced as part of the previous Government's National Energy Program revenuesharing scheme. That occurred for a number of reasons. First it was a tax on net revenues and not on profits. As such, it became a very blunt instrument for grabbing revenues for the federal Treasury. No recognition was given, for example, to the high capital costs associated with bringing on new oil and gas supplies. If anyone has taken the time to visit, as I have, some of the new exploration which is going on, not only in this country but in other countries as well, one would soon begin to realize the tremendous high capital costs which are associated with bringing on new oil and gas supplies. Second, the producing provinces as owners of the resources always objected to the federal Government imposing a discriminatory tax only on their industry and their resource. No special taxes were imposed on hydro, nickel or iron. They were just imposed on the resource of oil.
Third, to add insult to injury, the same income was taxed twice, once by the PGRT and then again by corporate income tax. Unexpected hardships resulted for many companies due to the double taxation of resource income. Most importantly, however, the PGRT reduced the incentive to reinvest because it was not profit sensitive. This insensitivity to profits led to a very poor investment climate and an unwillingness to invest in what otherwise might be attractive opportunities. The PGRT was a major factor which led to the downturn of the oil and gas investment activity after 1980. The Canadian reinvestment ratio in the petroleum industry fell from 147 per cent in 1980 to 83 per cent in 1983. That is a decline of nearly 45 per cent.
Western Canadian drilling activity in 1982 was 30 per cent below its 1980 level. Who can forget night after night seeing

In eastern Canada alone this has been measured to the extent of 9 per cent, this representing the contribution to acid rain formation by the emission of cars. The effects of acid rain are extremely well known to Canadians, Americans and Europeans. I will indicate the fact that forests are seriously damaged by the effects of acid rain, that buildings and structures are affected, that salmon spawning grounds are particularly affected in the springtime and that the combined effect of ozone on agriculture has already lead to considerable losses in production as measured in southwestern Ontario in particular. I should also mention that the impact of acid rain on sugar maple stands in Ontario and Quebec has been negative.
When we talk of acid rain we talk of a broad economic issue. We talk about damage done to a variety of natural resources. As well, we talk about the fact that our health is affected by this industrial phenomenon. When we consider the question of motivators we must include gasoline engines, diesel engines and the like.
The scale of the problem as covered by this particular motion applies only to the Hill because the Hill is a microcosm of the larger world beyond its gate. I am sure you have noticed that every day a considerable number of vehicles contribute to the problem of pollution on the Hill. I am told that up to 3,000 tour buses per year bring people to visit Parliament. There can be as many as 116 on a given day. Of course, the average is lower and the numbers vary through the year. Buses keep their engines idling while the passengers tour the Parliament Buildings.
There are several RCMP vehicles, marked and unmarked, as well as patrol cars which survey the premises from various vantage points. I have noticed, as you must have too, that when they are stationary they frequently leave their engines idling. There are some 40 Ministers' cars, probably the largest fleet in the history of Parliament. Depending on the weather, the car engines tend to be left running. The drivers sit in the cars when the weather is cold, or stand beside them, and leave the engines running while waiting for their next assignment.
The question, Mr. Speaker, is what are the solutions? We all realize that we have a cold climate and that we want to keep the cars warm. For that matter, we like to keep cars cool in the hot weather. However, let us deal with the cold weather because that is the most uncomfortable of the two. I would like to bring to your attention the fact that it is possible to buy fan heaters which run off the car's battery and provide adequate heat for people sitting in the car. These car heater units retail at approximately $70 apiece. It seems to me that every Canadian who is attracted by the idea of finding a solution to the problem of acid rain ought to think of the possibility of installing a car heater of this kind. This, of course, would apply mostly to the RCMP cars on the Hill and to the trucks that idle while delivering.
In the case of Ministerial drivers, I would suggest that provision could be made for them to wait in a room inside the buildings, thus eliminating the need for them to keep the engines running in order to be comfortable. With regard to the tour buses on the Hill, they ought to be asked by whoever is in charge of the parliamentary traffic division to turn their engines off in order to reduce discharges into the air which, as I mentioned earlier, are particularly strong in the summertime. There may be some discomfort for passengers who return to the bus and do not find the interior as cool as they would like, but it is a minor sacrifice considering the example that they would be setting to the nation by adhering to these rules.
It seems to me that MPs could also set an example on the Hill for Canadians to follow. Of course, in particular, cabinet Ministers may want to adopt the good practice of turning engines off when they are idling in the hope that this practice will be adopted and copied by others. In society we all take leadership for example, and there is definitely a lot of leadership that could be given by cabinet Ministers in this respect.
Outside the gates of Parliament Hill, Mr. Speaker, we would like to ask all Canadians to turn their engines off while waiting in their cars other than in normal driving patterns. This applies to all vehicles, but it seems to me that it would have a particular impact in bus terminals and at taxi stands.
If this motion were to be adopted, it would be necessary to have a public education program. That initiative would require provincial and municipal co-operation with the federal Government. I submit that the three levels of Government should promote the idea of shutting off engines through an advertising campaign which could be carried out in local newspapers, by way of radio and even television. Parallel to that, Mr. Speaker, there could be a campaign of stickers promoting the fact the driver of a vehicle is concerned about acid rain. The slogan could read: "I do not idle. I fight acid rain". In the towns, villages, and cities across Canada we could also seek the co-operation of driving schools which could promote this idea while instructing new drivers. There could be another form of public education with the help of service clubs which could be asked to reward environmentally conscious drivers through a variety of initiatives at certain times of the year. This would stress the fact that keeping emissions to a minimum while idling has long-term beneficial effects on human health.
The Department of the Environment, at the federal level, could launch an annual contest among schools across Canada in which the young people in the schools, our future drivers, could develop creative ideas on how to reduce the habit of idling a car while waiting. While this is not exclusively an urban problem, it is magnified by the larger number of vehicles in urban situations.
In summary, eliminating the habit of idling a car engine needlessly is one important way in which every Canadian car owner can contribute to the reduction of acid rain. Of course, there are other methods, including using unleaded gasoline, accelerating moderately, frequently checking tire pressure,
November 18, 1985

observing speed limits and tuning the engine regularly. Last, but not least, it is increasingly important to install a three way catalytic converter which has the effect of virtually eliminating the nitrogen oxide emissions of a car whether idling or running on the roads. This would considerably reduce the negative effects of pollution that results from the running of a combustion engine.
I am using the example of idling the engine of a car as a symbolic measure and I am using the territory covered by Parliament Hill as a symbolic area. If we were to combine all of these preventive measures, we would go a long way to reducing the extent of acid rain in our country. At the same time, we would make our cars run better. By reducing that pollution, we also reduce the emission of toxic substances into the air which eventually returns to the soil, our crops and forests by means of that acid rain which does so much damage.
By asking Canadians to participate in a campaign to eliminate the habit of idling engines when possible, we would be asking each Canadian who cares to become a real and active participant in the battle against acid rain. It is something, as small as it may seem and as small as it really is, that we can do about acid rain in our country. This is a specific example that I would like to put forward tonight to the House for the consideration of Hon. Members.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words to the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). It is a good motion for a number of reasons. First, it illustrates how all of us can participate in ways that are helpful to the environment. It is not only a question of large policy changes with respect to Government or questions of industrial environmental policy, it is also a question of how we behave as individuals in everyday situations and habits.
It is worthy to remember that we all have a role to play in confronting air pollution and other environmental questions. It can take the form of ensuring that we dispose of empty cans rather than throwing them on the side of the road or not idling our engines unnecessarily. It is certainly true that this occurs on Parliament Hill, particularly with the tour buses and Ministers' cars. I do not have a car so I have not given much thought to this in terms of my own habits. However, I congratulate the Hon. Member for bringing this issue to the floor of the House of Commons.
I must caution him that the real reductions in air pollution will take place when we have the kind of pollution abatement programs that so many of us in the House have asked for from the last Government and the present Government. Those are the programs that will make the real difference in terms of over-all reduction of emissions.
We should be careful not to get involved in blaming the victims of this problem and transferring the responsibility for the quality of our environment to individuals while forgetting that the most serious environmental pollution comes from the action of industry in our environment and economy. It is important to focus our attention in that area rather than
Environmental Affairs
concentrate on how individuals contribute to environmental pollution. I am not saying that individual participation is not important but we should not shift our attention from what can be done by Government policy about the various sources of pollution.
I remind Hon. Members that we have not seen any concrete manifestation of the hopes that were aroused when the Government announced that it was prepared to contribute $150 million with the provinces toward the acid rain problem. I understand that an announcement is forthcoming and I hope it will be beneficial, but we have yet to see something concrete take place at that level.
There has been opportunity to take steps in this context during a recent debate on the question of leaded and unleaded gasoline. I support the views of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) about the need for Canadians to use more unleaded gas but I regret that he has not taken the opportunities to use legislation before the House to do something about the tax framework applied to leaded and unleaded gasoline. I do not believe there would be any political repercussions-unless it affects the oil companies-to provide an equal price for leaded and unleaded gasoline. I would prefer to see a disincentive for using leaded gasoline by making it more expensive, but why could they not be the same price to at least provide incentive for people to use unleaded gasoline?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on the motion by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) and to make a few comments contrary to those made by the previous Member. The actions taken by the Government to control vehicle emissions are only part of the picture. They are only one element of a larger program to combat air pollution on all fronts. Measures already taken by this Government will reduce harmful emissions of nitrogen oxide. They will also greatly curtail the amounts of hydrocarbons, carbon monoxide and lead. The new standards will have the effect of reducing automotive pollution by over 45 per cent by the end of the century.
The Government is moving against air pollution to protect the health of Canadians, to improve air quality, particularly in our urban areas, to reduce crop losses caused by automotive pollutants and to control the greatest environmental problems that Canada has ever faced, namely, acid rain.
Acid rain is caused by two common by-products of our modern industrial lifestyle, sulphur oxide and nitrogen oxides. As a result of acid rain, or more correctly acid precipitation, the rains and snows that once were clean and pristine have now become dangerously acidic and destructive due to human activity.
The main sources of sulphur oxide emissions in North America are coal fired power generating stations and non-ferrous ore smelters. The main sources of nitrogen oxide emissions are vehicles. The Government's initiative to clean up acid rain will vastly reduce sulphur emissions as well. In fact, the Canadian acid rain control program announced on March 6 is the most ambitious environmental program that has ever been launched in this country.
Consider, Mr. Speaker, the accomplishments of this program. Canada is the only country to have based an acid rain control policy on achieving a quantifiable environmental objective, the target loading level of 20 kilograms per hectare per year of wet sulphate fallout, the level which our lakes and rivers can tolerate without damage occurring.
Canada's commitment to reduce sulphur dioxide emissions in eastern Canada by 50 per cent by the year 1994 is the largest percentage cut-back promised by any national acid rain program. The Government has put in place a pragmatic program to see that this commitment will be fulfilled. Our new motor vehicle emissions are as tough as those of any other nation in the world and, indeed, are tougher than most.
The program of the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) includes the largest and most comprehensive scientific research and monitoring effort ever undertaken by Canada in the environmental field. Current expenditures equal $30 million, and over $18 million of this sum will come from the federal Government.
In a way which typifies the working of the new Government, Canada's acid rain program is an example of co-operation. It involves the seven eastern provincial Governments in the signing of agreements with the federal Government and the active support of the three western provinces. As well, the program reflects the interests of the private sector and of citizens of all ages and walks of life.
Each of these provincial Governments has now identified the S02 emissions to be cut to safeguard the Canadian environment from acid rain and each has committed itself to make these cuts. The process of developing regulatory orders is now under way.
The Province of Quebec provides a good example of how the acid rain agreement will work in a practical way. Quebec announced its emission control plans on February 8, 1985, in amendments to its Environmental Quality Act. Quebec's sulphur emissions will be cut back by 45 per cent over-all. In some cases, actions must be initiated immediately to respond to the regulations. The implementation of these regulations means that Quebec will have done its share in helping Canada to meet its 1994 reduction target. The other eastern provincial Governments are expected to announce their own emission control regulations during 1985.
These measures to reduce acid rain will not be without cost. The price of designing and installing acid rain control measures is over $1.5 billion, of which $750 million will be spent in the nickel and copper smelting industry.
Industry has the primary responsibility for carrying these costs. The federal and provincial Governments have agreed to provide financial assistance in cases where a company cannot afford to implement the necessary pollution control measures as quickly as required to meet society's best interests.
The Government, Mr. Speaker, has been able to sit down with the provinces, discuss the acid rain problem in a frank and realistic manner, a portion of the cut-backs that are necessary to meet the 1994 targets and hammer out a way to meet the substantial costs involved.
We are supporting technology development for the cleaner and more efficient use of coal for power generation. The objective of this program is to make the continued use of coal, particularly Canadian coal, economically attractive for power generation by both industry and utilities within the established emission levels. More than $70 million has been budgeted for this purpose over the next four years. Together with the western coal producing provinces and Ontario, we are investigating the prospects for using low sulphur western coal in Ontario.
We are also pledged to a continuing scientific investigation and monitoring of acid rain. Annual expenditures in this field will be in excess of $18 million, and will involve Government scientists and engineers from eight different departments and agencies. The private sector and our universities will be asked to join in this work.
The Hon. Member's motion states that:
-the Government should launch a public education campaign inviting all Canadians to do the same and to invite the provincial Governments to take the same steps.
November 18, 1985

In other words, the motion is calling upon the Government to get involved and to educate the Canadian public about better driving habits. I am pleased to inform this House that Environment Canada is already active in the area of vehicle emissions and good driving practices, including excessive idling of cars. I would like to call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to just two of the Department's fact sheets, one entitled Air Pollution and Your Car and the other Winter Driving. Both are excellent brochures. Both warn against excessive idling. Last April's issue of Environment Update was devoted exclusively to the automobile and the responsibilities of the user in helping to protect the environment. As well, there are a number of publications put out by the Department of Transport and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources encouraging good driving habits. Of particular note is Transport Canada's 1986 Fuel Consumption Guide which rates new cars' performance and includes reference to low polluting cars.
I hope I have shown that the Government's program to fight acid rain by reducing emissions from various sources, including cars, is a sign of its commitment to environmental quality in general. The Government has been given the wherewithal to carry out its resolve to clean up our environment through the assurance of a stable Budget and sound government finances for at least the next five years.
The Hon. Member's motion is completely in line with the policies and practices of the Government. It brings home to all of us, in a very concrete way, the aims and goals toward which we are working and sets an example for the way in which individual actions of ordinary Canadians can be brought to bear to reduce air pollution. I support the motion and recommend that it be adopted.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS ABANDONMENT OF PRACTICE OF LEAVING CAR ENGINES RUNNING ON PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know whether we are on the verge of doing something here which will dramatically affect our life-styles as Members of Parliament. I guess that remains to be seen. We become a part of a very select group of people in the House of Commons after six o'clock in the evening. I guess we will not all have to walk home.
We have before us a very interesting and worth-while proposal by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). Other Hon. Members have supported his motion quite freely. He is asking us, as Members of Government and specifically as Members of Parliament, to set an example which will show Canadians at large that we are serious about the kinds of things we discuss, not only tonight but whenever we talk about environmental issues. Basically he asks us to practise what we preach in this specific area which is under our domain.
A couple of points might be made. I am not sure whether the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) raised some concern as to the balance between private Canadian citizens and Canadian industries on the relative contribution which each might make to air pollution. I do not know whether it is an either-or situation. I do not know whether he
Environmental Affairs
meant to imply that. However, I do not think the motion indicates that it will solve all our problems.
Depending upon what area of the country one looks at, a very significant proportion of the problem is caused by automobile emissions. Probably Los Angeles might be the best example in the world, but we certainly have our own examples in Canada. In some of the downtown core areas of our cities this motion could make a dramatic difference. I think Ottawa itself would be well served if the motion was concurred in.
The motion before the House is very similar to a suggestion brought before us not long ago. I do not have the exact date, but it was presented by the Chairman of the Special Subcommittee on Acid Rain, the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Mus-koka (Mr. Darling). Under the provisions of Standing Order 21 he asked the House for unanimous approval to ensure that the buses about which the Hon. Member for Davenport spoke, would no longer idle the way they do.
This raises a very specific point which the Chair might like to consider. There may in fact be instances where there is reason for it not being an absolute rule, where common sense might prevail. For example, it might involve a refrigeration unit containing Hershey bars, or some other very perishable product which requires refrigeration to avoid spoilage or destruction of edible foodstuffs. It may not be the only example. There could be other very specific instances. I am sure Hon. Members have confidence in the discretion of the Chair to ensure that whatever the House decides in its wisdom to pass will be executed with some common sense and in a reasonable way.
What stands out in my mind-and perhaps it stands out in the minds of other Hon. Members or perhaps the scribes who are listening-is that this has been going on for a long time. It is not a new problem which we discuss in the House tonight, it has been going on for years and there can be no question in anyone's mind about that. If we take a look at the figures and the information now available to us we will see that air pollution is an ongoing and very serious problem which we in Canada have been trying to come to grips with for many years.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill asked where was the action about which we had talked. When the Conservative Government came into power on September 4, 1984, we promised an action plan within six months. The last Minister of the Environment delivered that action plan on time, and in a way which provided effective control in one specific area of air pollution. Included in that control program were significant changes, as indicated by the previous speaker, to acceptable levels of auto emissions. We have expectations that we will see the Final touches to that program, the action plan which was presented in full along with the federal commitment, in the very near future. It will be a relief for all of us. Then we will be left to deal with the major problems of trans-boundary pollution.
We know that automobile emissions account for 21 per cent of all man-made Canadian nitrogen oxide emissions. Other transportation vehicles, including heavy-duty trucks, machines and off-highway transport, produce 41 per cent of NO, emis-

November 18, 1985
Environmental Affairs
sions, so that vehicular transport accounts for 62 per cent of NO, emissions in Canada. If we balance that with the industry component, we find that it does not account for all the remaining, but certainly vehicles account for the majority of emissions, and individual Canadians drive those vehicles.
Nitrogen emissions are a dangerous environmental pollutant. I should like to touch upon several matters, but first I would like to review the environmental problems associated with NO,. Some of this terminology may confuse some people from time to time, myself included, but NO, includes a whole range of oxides of nitrogen. They are grouped or clumped together in this so-called NO,. All of them have their own level of danger. Some are more dangerous in certain situations than others. There are direct and indirect effects. The direct effects are on human health, on the environment itself and on material goods. We heard a little from the Hon. Member for Davenport about the effects on human health. Primarily we should consider the effect on the respiratory tract itself.
Also we have seen the effects which nitrogen oxide can have on plants, particularly commercially grown crops. However, there is good evidence to show, especially as a component of acid rain, that not only commercial plants are affected. In some areas of the country-the area in which I live, for instance-acid rain and its effect on small lakes is not really a problem because of a limestone base. Therefore, people in those areas do not have the same sensitivity to the issue as those in other parts of Ontario, or indeed Canada.
When acidic precipitation becomes heavy enough, it affects the leaves on trees, and on other plants growing around homes for example. In fact, leaves experience significant detrimental impact from highly acidic rain.
The indirect effects relate to the reaction of nitrogen oxides with other elements of air pollution. We are all familiar with smog. We usually think of it in terms of very large cities, but smog is formed when nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons combine. They, together with other products of combustion, react with sunlight. A major component of smog is ozone.
If it is difficult for myself or other people to communicate some of this information, it is because we do not exactly know what we are talking about. That is not to say that we do not have good reason to respond or to take action, but the scientific evidence is certainly incomplete. It is not developed to a point where we can precisely indicate the reaction of specific by-products or a combination thereof. We know the end effect of many of these things. We know, for instance, the very serious effect which ozone can have on our agricultural products in Ontario. There are $2 billion worth of agricultural product affected each year and the losses to agriculture in Ontario are as high as $20 million a year just from ozone alone. We know that 7 per cent of people when exposed to ozone have very serious respiratory problems. So there is a health impact as well as a direct impact on other living material such as plants. We know of some specific problems but are unfortunately not in a position to be completely clear on all of these interactions.
Ozone levels in many Canadian cities have exceeded the national ambient air quality objectives which we believe are acceptable. A specific example which impressed me is that Vancouverites are frequently exposed to elevated ozone levels once or twice a week during the summer months. In eastern Canada, particularly in southwestern Ontario, high ozone levels are related to the trans-boundary movement of air pollution. We know as well, and we have heard information on it today, that the NO emissions themselves must be reduced in order to address the acid rain problem in Canada. NO emissions are responsible for about 35 per cent of the acidity of precipitation. In winter months, they can be responsible for up to 50 per cent of the acidity of precipitation. Nitrates deposited during the winter months accumulate in the snow pack and when the snow melts accumulated acid from the nitrates then runs off into the so-called spring shock. This gets into our lakes, streams and watersheds and in those higher concentrations picks up some of the heavy metals which themselves contribute to some of the secondary effects of acid rain and the resultant effects on our forests.
Evidence is mounting which suggests that the combined effects of acid rain, ozone and climatic stress such as drought can combine in ways which are highly damaging, particularly to forests. Dramatic evidence of these effects has already emerged, particularly in Europe. Germany, in particular, has responded very dramatically. It has had almost a complete turn-around in its whole environmental program and concepts within the last two or three years. Its current policy now calls for substantial reductions in both sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxide emissions.
NO, emissions in Canada have been increasing steadily. In fact, it is predicted that if they are not controlled by the end of the century they will rise to a level 20 per cent higher than they are now. In view of the fact that these emissions have been increasing at such rates that they damage the environment and contribute to acid rain, controls on NO, emissions in Canada are urgently needed.
The Conservative Government has recognized this need and after years and years of inaction a package of measures was introduced last March which we feel can be effective in reducing these emissions to an acceptable level in order to prevent further damage from the acid precipitation.
I could talk about some of the things we have accomplished in gazetting the standards we hope we can achieve and plan on achieving. The second part of the gazetting which would impose those standards is currently being considered now and we hope to introduce it very shortly.
I would like to conclude by making a few points which I believe are important. The question of lead in our gasoline has already been alluded to. This is a part of the total emissions from cars here on the Hill and everywhere right across Canada. We know of the effects of this on human health. What I want to do is specifically mention something which I do not believe has been mentioned before, that is, in September of 1984 the previous Minister of the Environment in this
November 18, 1985

Government asked the Royal Society of Canada to provide independent advice on the present and future risks resulting from the presence of lead in the environment.
The Royal Society Commission on Lead in the environment released its report on October 29, 1985, less than a month ago. The recommendations in the report support the planned reduction of lead in leaded gasoline and the stricter exhaust emission controls for new vehicles which will take effect in 1987. The report also states that the Minister may want to reduce levels of lead in gasoline even further. The Minister has declared his intention to meet with members of the petroleum industry to discuss a timetable for the phase-out of lead in gasoline.
What we have before us, Mr. Speaker, is a very common sense and reasonable motion. We, as a Government, are determined to protect the health of Canadians and our environment as far as possible. We want to encourage all actions toward this end. I believe, Mr. Speaker, if you were to ask for concurrence in this motion you would find the House to be in agreement.
I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Davenport for his foresight and his ongoing efforts on behalf of the environment and I would like to assure him that the Government plans to follow along with things which have been initiated in the past and also to proceed in the future to make sure that we have the kind of environment which will serve us all well.

subtopic: CHILDREN-PROPOSAL TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL CENTRE FOR MISSING CHILDREN
CHILDREN-PROPOSAL TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL CENTRE FOR MISSING CHILDREN
speechtext:
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, we have a very major problem in this country, that of missing children. Some of the children run away from home, some of them are abducted by their parents and some of them are abducted by strangers. Over the last 10 years in Metropolitan Toronto, apart from those children who were abducted by their parents, some 64,000 cases of missing children were reported. On almost any day in Metropolitan Toronto between 35 and 75 children are reported missing. Of course, this is a problem not only in Metropolitan Toronto, it exists right across the country. There are thousands and thousands of cases of missing children reported each year.
What are we currently doing about this situation? Some of the police departments are very co-operative assisting the parents in trying to track down missing children. Some police departments are not quite as co-operative. Police departments are linked by a computer system, and the Canadian Police Information Centre tries to keep track of all police information, including missing children. Unfortunately there is no common data base between police departments with respect to matters relating to missing children. As a result, it is impossible for the police to access this information accurately and properly to every police department in the country when they need it. We have and continue to have the problem of a lack of information relating to missing children.
In the United States they have tried to meet this problem by establishing the National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children. On October 10, you will remember, Mr. Speaker, that I asked a question of the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Beatty) relating to the American Centre, and whether he would consider establishing a similar centre in Canada. Subsequently I wrote to him on the same subject.
In his reply on November 1, he indicated that he currently has the Royal Canadian Mounted Police doing extensive work on the question of establishing a central registry for missing children, a registry that would provide, in his words: first, enhancement of police investigations concerning missing children; second, a mechanism through which the public would seek information on missing children; and third, a mechanism which would facilitate the correlation of information with a view to periodically publishing national bulleting on missing children and other forms of public information. This is something that is certainly long overdue.
I have received a letter from a Mr. Gary Rosenfeldt, Director of the Victims of Violence, an organization centred in Edmonton. He mentioned one case involving a missing child in which he has been involved. He tried to communicate with the police department in one particular city on this subject, asking for a picture of the missing child that has actually been published in the press. He did not receive any response whatsoever to his letter. He called long distance asking for a picture of the missing child and was promised a picture, but it never

November 18, 1985
Adjournment Debate
came. Eventually, he received a picture from private sources. The Victims of Violence organization publish flyers and leaflets on which pictures of missing children are printed, and using volunteers they have been posted in some 8,000 post offices across the country. That is the sort of thing that is very helpful, but certainly the police should be much more active and helpful in this area.
In his letter of November 1 the Solicitor General went on to say that the registry he has in mind on which the RCMP is working would not be the equivalent of the National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children in the United States. That American centre was established in 1984 and was funded with something like $4 million. It is an organization that is centred within the United States Department of Justice. It administers this system which helps to co-ordinate a volunteer network looking for missing children, a free telephone system to carry the information and a whole network that provides information relating to missing children so that the public, parents and anyone interested can receive this information. This organization has been in existence for a very short period of time but hopefully it will have the effect that all of us wish to see, of helping to locate missing children, whether they are missing as a result of running away or of abduction.
In his letter the Solicitor General went on to say that he has also instructed officials in his own Department to carry on discussions with the Department of Justice and the Department of National Health and Welfare with a view to examining further initiatives that might be taken by the federal Government, either alone or in conjunction with the provinces and the private sector, to alleviate the human tragedy associated with the phenomenon of missing children. That is certainly something in which we are all interested. Hopefully the efforts of the Solicitor General of Canada will bear some results.
I am optimistic that we will see some legislation to assist, and that we will definitely see a registry of missing children. I hope there will be other measures as well to help solve this very, very perplexing and troublesome problem. I am looking forward to hearing the Parliamentary Secretary tonight tell us of his suggestions and hopefully the suggestions of the Solicitor General of Canada regarding what immediate action will be taken by the Government in this direction to help solve the tragic problem of missing children in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul Dick (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: CHILDREN-PROPOSAL TO ESTABLISH NATIONAL CENTRE FOR MISSING CHILDREN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to expand on the reply given October 10, 1985 by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) to the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) regarding the establishment of a national centre to assist in locating missing children. The Hon. Minister of Justice informed the House that the RCMP is presently exploring the feasibility of establishing a national registry to assist in the search for missing children. In addition, I would like to elaborate briefly on the efforts of our U.S. neighbours, and also to describe an important piece of legislation presently under consideration by this Government that will assist in locating children abducted by parents.
The National Centre for Missing and Exploited Children in Washington, D.C. is located within the federal Justice Department and largely co-ordinates efforts of local law-enforcement agencies and volunteer groups to assist in locating missing children. It has in place a toll-free number for the public to use in order to report children who have gone missing and the sightings of any missing children. It is also involved in promoting public education and public awareness programs about the problem of missing children.
For example, it promotes the training of law-enforcement officers and members of the legal profession in a way that would inform them about the realities of missing children. Its staff does not actually search for missing children. However, it has access to the National Crime Information Computer system and other networks to facilitate its work. The success of the centre's co-ordination efforts therefore relies heavily on existing law-enforcement facilities and adequate laws throughout the United States. Without the capacity to obtain reports on missing children and to be able to call on law-enforcement and social agency personnel to carry out the search, a coordinating service such as this would not be able to achieve the desired results. This should make it clear to the Hon. Member that, while a central co-ordinating centre has an important role to play, it plays only a small part in the over-all network that must also be in place.
I would now like to say a few words about our own federal efforts to introduce a similar co-ordinating mechanism at the federal level designed to assist in the tracing of missing children in Canada. The Minister of Justice has sponsored a Bill that is presently under consideration by the Government which, if passed, will allow courts to authorize the release of information to trace missing persons. It would apply to cases in which children are missing due to parental abductions, and also to cases in which children are missing due to the violation of a custody order, a right-of-access order or a custody agreement. It is expected that these provisions will increase the enforceability of parental abduction offences recently introduced into the Criminal Code, as well as secure greater respect for custody and access rights.
[ Translation]

subtopic: TEXTILES (A) INQUIRY ABOUT $30 MILLION GIVEN TO DOMINION TEXTILE (B) INQUIRY RESPECTING USE OF FUNDS PAID TO DOMINION TEXTILE
TEXTILES (A) INQUIRY ABOUT $30 MILLION GIVEN TO DOMINION TEXTILE (B) INQUIRY RESPECTING USE OF FUNDS PAID TO DOMINION TEXTILE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, regarding the question I put to the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Bissonnette) on October 30 of this year concerning the textile industry and more specifically: " .. . the shutdown of two modern plants in Saint-Jean and Valleyfield, the members of a committee to maintain employment urged the Government to inquire into the use and management of public funds given to Dominion Textile by the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board." And my question was: "Was there an inquiry? If so, what has been learned about the $30 million given to Dominion Textiles?"
November 18, 1985

Mr. Speaker, to give some background information and provide some insight into the importance of this issue, I would like to start by talking about the social and economic impact of Dominion Textile's decision to close its two plants. With an unemployment rate near 12 per cent in both communities, the social and economic repercussions of the shutdown of these plants could prove to be disastrous for Saint-Jean and Valley-field.
The two support committees estimate that in addition to the 850 employees, union and management, who will be laid off, there are some 1,200 people, dependent children and spouses, who will also be directly affected. The total wage bill at stake in the case of a shutdown would be around $20 million. Add to this the subsequent loss of at least 200 jobs indirectly related to the industry.
The impact would be even more severe in the Valleyfield area, according to Denis Lecompte, Vice-President of the Chamber of Commerce, since the average age of employees at the Valleyfield plant is 42.8, which is higher than in Saint-Jean, where the average age is 33.5, which means Valleyfield workers would have more trouble finding new employment. This particular impact, this economic fact was described in a document prepared by the committee for maintaining jobs in Valleyfield and Saint-Jean-sur-le-Richelieu.
Mr. Speaker, I also want to quote from an article that appeared in May 1984. The Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), at the time Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party and of the Official Opposition, said as reported in the Sherbrooke newspaper La Tribune:
A Conservative Government would not get rid of the import quotas imposed by Canada in the footwear and textile sectors.
"The quota policy will remain as is", declared Mr. Mulroney, who said he was not in favour of free trade in these particular sectors.
He added that he would not "give in" to pressure from Common Market countries and the United States to reduce quotas on footwear or textile products imported into Canada.
"And I will certainly say so to President Reagan when 1 meet him in Washington next month. I will make sure our interests are protected at all times. Friendship does not come free. Neighbours like us are worth a lot", maintained the Conservative Leader.
Mr. Speaker, the situation has taken a turn for the worst. Over 800 jobs will disappear. The average age of workers is 42.8 in Valleyfield and 33.5 in Saint-Jean-sur-le-Richelieu. They can therefore expect to have some retraining problems.
The current buzz words are free trade, but the fact is that Canadian taxpayers have put up $30 million to enable Dominion Textile to equip its two plants with the most modern facilities in Canada, yet they will be the first to close down.
Now then, as I said in my supplementary question to the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Bissonnette) on October 30, 1985: What happens to the $30 million-and these funds belong to Canadian taxpayers-paid to Dominion Textile which has now announced the shutdowns? What happens to that money, Mr. Speaker?
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Paul Dick (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: TEXTILES (A) INQUIRY ABOUT $30 MILLION GIVEN TO DOMINION TEXTILE (B) INQUIRY RESPECTING USE OF FUNDS PAID TO DOMINION TEXTILE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to reply to the question put by the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) who was concerned about $30 million supposedly paid to Dominion Textile which recently announced the closing of its Saint-Jean and Valleyfield plants.
An important element of the textile and clothing policy announced in June 1981 was the establishment of the Canadian Industrial Renewal Board. The purpose of this board is to provide firms in these sectors with financial assistance to enable them to restructure and modernize their facilities.
In February, 1983 the CIRB approved an offer of a contribution to Dominion Textile based on the intention of the company to invest $150 million. To date, eligible capital expenditures by the company have totalled $79,101,011, for which the company has received a contribution of $15,820,202, corresponding to 20 per cent of approved expenditures. The company has until June 30, 1986 to complete its project. It is not expected that the company will be able to finalize its restructuring plan as forecasted.
With respect to the assistance provided to the two plants for which closures are scheduled for June 1986, totals of $2,337,048 and $286,905 were disbursed for the Saint-Jean and Valleyfield plants respectively. There is nothing in the agreement with the company which prevents the movement of assisted assets from one location to another, as long as they continue to be utilized by the company to improve its competitiveness, the prime objective of the CIRB program.
As part of the process of restructuring its activities, the firm has chosen to rationalize its operations further by closing the Saint-Jean and Valleyfield plants. We understand most of the equipment, which is fairly modern, will be transferred to other plants owned by the company. CIRB will not finance the moving of the equipment. From a total of 740 jobs which will be affected in Saint-Jean and Valleyfield the company expects to provide some 350 to 400 extra jobs in Drummondville and Magog. It is hoped that these measures taken by Dominion Textile will result in a return to profitability and the safeguard of the 7,000 jobs which remain in the company.
Although the company has confirmed that its decision to close the two plants is final I can assure the Hon. Member that the Government is continuing to explore, with the company and persons concerned, all the options available for keeping these plants in operation or for attracting additional investment in order to maintain an equivalent number of jobs. Various factors contributed to these two plant closures including increased imports.
The Government is currently reviewing the situation of the textile and clothing industry with a view to developing a revised textile and clothing policy. The policy review is aimed at developing measures to provide longer term certainty for these industries and their employees. It will also include an assessment of the multi-fibre arrangement which provides a

November 18, 1985
Adjournment Debate
framework for regulating international trade in textile and clothing products.

subtopic: FISHERIES-STANDING COMMITTEE HEARINGS. (B) EFFECT OF LICENSING FACTORY FREEZER TRAWLER
FISHERIES-STANDING COMMITTEE HEARINGS. (B) EFFECT OF LICENSING FACTORY FREEZER TRAWLER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to elaborate on a question I asked of the Acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Nielsen) concerning the licensing of factory freezer trawlers in Atlantic Canada.
At the time the committee was travelling in Atlantic Canada there was only one application under active consideration. That was for National Sea Products Limited to operate a factory freezer trawler off the East Coast of Canada. In our opinion, the information gathered in that committee was gathered behind closed doors without public input and public scrutiny of the process. Of the approximate 106 witnesses who appeared before the committee, the vast majority were absolutely opposed to the granting of a factory freezer licence and saw very serious impacts for Atlantic Canada if it were granted.
The committee travelled through Atlantic Canada between October 23 and November 6 and there were requests to raise the matter. By and large the committee denied those requests and would not permit a detailed hearing of the factory freezer trawler issue. Instead, the committee passed a unanimous motion to hold a one-day hearing in Ottawa on November 21. An advertisement was placed in the newspapers of Atlantic Canada asking for the submission of briefs from groups affected and interested in this particular question. The opposition was so virtually unanimous and so deeply rooted in Atlantic Canada that certainly this should have been done. Unfortunately, the Conservative members of the committee decided today that they would not permit the groups affected and the people of Atlantic Canada to comment on the impact of this licensing. I am not speaking of just one licence but three. We feel it is an incredible breach of confidence in the committee and a breach of the parliamentary process when a committee can unanimously turn around and cut off all input which would occur in a public forum.
We in the Opposition see this as the hand of the Acting Minister of Fisheries, a man whom I would suggest has been given the task of dismantling many of the aspects of Government. We wonder whether or not one of his tasks is the dismantling of the Atlantic fishery through the method by which the Government has chosen to license the factory freezer trawlers. We see the hand of the Acting Minister through the Parliamentary Secretary who gave the direction or the marching orders to Conservative members of the committee to vote against allowing the people and groups they represent from Altantic Canada from appearing before the committee and laying out the problems they have or, in some cases, the support they have for the factory freezer trawler issue. By and large the vast majority of Atlantic Canadians involved in the fishing industry are absolutely opposed to this move.
I would like to mention a couple of small items in addition to the very negative impact on the rural fishing communities
and the inshore fisheries of the Provinces of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. I am referring to the situation in St. Pierre and Miquelon where the French are attempting to use factory freezer trawlers in the area around St. Pierre and Miquelon. Canada has recently submitted that case to arbitration. I think the Canadians have made fools of themselves in the international theatre by grating not only one licence but three for factory freezer trawlers, considering the timing of the granting of these licences prior to an arbitration case. 1 think they have cut their own throats on this particular matter, an act of colossal stupidity.
As well, we are talking about free trade with the United States. It has been said in the U.S. that if we want greater access to that market we should be prepared to allow the Americans to fish our surplus stock with factory freezer trawlers. They would not have to worry about jobs in Canada. They will deliver our fish in their vessels into their ports for their market.
Again, the Acting Minister of Fisheries, with undignified haste, is attempting to muzzle the committee and by doing so demonstrates contempt for parliamentary reform. It demonstrates contempt for the committee system. This Governmenl obviously has no intention of abiding by a policy of open Government. The decisions will be taken by someone who is literally the hit man for this Government behind closed doors.
We suspect that the reason for this muzzling is to allow the dirty work to be done by the Acting Minister. Should the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) ever get around to appointing a new Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, one who is concerned about the industry on both coasts, he will supposedly be able to approach the job with clean hands. However, that is not going to happen. If we cannot deal with this matter in committee, we intend to raise the issue time after time after time in this House. This issue must be dealt with properly in a public forum before a decision is made which will literally take apart many of our small communities in Atlantic Canada.
